_doc: T-0839. ONE PERSON, SEVERAL CARDS: the written ruling on every cluster of town cards that a surname-plus-compatible-forename test joins. The owner, 2026-09-05, reading the households folder: 'do a review and consolidate of the residents, like James Allen is almost certainly one record and he is spread across several, don't lose any data, but consolidation is needed across the residents' — and, when the first draft of this ticket stopped at a report, 'make the ticket merge those records — research without consolidation is useless'. This file is the RULING; tools/consolidate_town_cards.py derives the candidate clusters from the committed cards, refuses to pass its gate while any card in a candidate cluster carries no ruling here, and lands the merges. A ruling is a claim and carries its reasoning: `for` is the evidence the two cards name one person, `against` is what would say otherwise, and both are written even where the answer is obvious, because the next pass reads this instead of re-asking.

rules.C0: THE OWNER RULED IT. T-0839 names Allen, Hubbard, Owen, Fullerton, Kimberly and Haddock as merges in the ticket body: 'where the evidence is one man with a title, an initial and a full name, it is a MERGE'. This pass does not re-litigate them.
rules.C1: THE SAME NAME, TWICE. Two cards whose forenames are the same word or an unambiguous expansion of it, on the same source and the same date. Nothing distinguishes them at all.
rules.C2: AN INITIAL ONTO ITS ONE FULL FORENAME. The abbreviated card's initials agree letter for letter with the full-name card's, no middle initial contradicts, and exactly ONE full forename in the cluster carries the initial. Two rivals is a refusal, not a coin toss — the rule the newspapers' identity.json already ratified.
rules.C3: A BARE FORENAME ONTO AN ANCHOR. One card names a person the town DOCUMENTS — a trade, an arrival, a dwelling, a source that is not a bare list — and the other prints the same forename and surname with nothing that contradicts it, and the anchor is the only bearer of that forename in the cluster.
rules.C4: A CONTRADICTED MIDDLE INITIAL, OVER AN ANCHOR. The cluster holds one documented bearer of the forename, at least one card carries his full name, and the variation is confined to the middle initial across manuscript lists that a copyist mis-set. This is the rule the owner applied to Haddock (E / E. W. / Edward E. / Edward H.) and it is applied no further than that shape.
rules.R1: SURNAME AND A TITLE IS NOT A NAME. A card that prints no forename cannot be attached to one — the refusal data/research/newspapers/identity.json has ratified since the press pass.
rules.R2: TWO RIVALS IS A REFUSAL. An initial that could expand to two full forenames in the same cluster attaches to neither.
rules.R3: A CONTRADICTED MIDDLE INITIAL, WITH NO ANCHOR. Neither card documents the person beyond a list, and the two printed middle initials disagree. Either two men or one man mis-set, and nothing reached decides which.
rules.R4: A BARE FORENAME WITH NO ANCHOR. Neither card documents the person, so there is nothing for the bare forename to attach to. T-0696 is the ticket that would give this test a second discriminator.
rules.R5: A GARBLED FORENAME CANNOT BE TESTED. T-0695 is the ticket that reads them.
rules.D1: TWO PEOPLE THE SOURCES NAME SEPARATELY. A spouse, a sibling, a parent and child, or two explicit and different forenames.
rules.D2: A DATE CONTRADICTION. One card's person is dead, or absent, on a day the other's is documented alive in the town.
rules.C5: THE TRANSCRIBER NAMED HIM, IN BRACKETS. A reading that carries a bracketed forename — 'Hubbard, [Henry] G.' — is an editorial expansion by whoever transcribed the source: somebody looked at the page and said who this is. That names the person directly, so it outranks any inference drawn from the initials, and in particular it settles a cluster C2 would REFUSE for having two rivals. The bracket is evidence about identity; the initial is only evidence about spelling. Applied no further than a forename the transcription itself supplies.
rules.U1: UNDECIDED, AND THE QUESTION IS FILED. Two cards a candidate test joins where the answer needs a reading of the page rather than a rule — both readings are stated, neither is taken, and a ticket owns it. An undecided cluster still satisfies the gate, because the gate asks that a cluster be WEIGHED, not that it be merged.
rules.D3: A FEMALE HONORIFIC ON A MAN'S OWN NAME. `Mrs Rufus Brown` is not Rufus Brown. The honorific is stripped before two names are compared, which leaves the husband's forename tokens standing on both readings and makes the pair identical; a woman whose only printed name is her husband's is a real and common shape in this corpus and she is never her husband. The refusal is the card-side statement of R6 in tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py, which holds the two identities apart in the derivation, and it fires on the same evidence: a SOURCE that prints both readings as separate entries (T-0723).
rules.D4: THE CARDS STAY TWO BECAUSE NOTHING JOINS THEM. Two printings of one surname whose middle initials disagree, where C4 cannot fire — either no anchor exists, or the anchor's own record cannot reach the other card's date. This is NOT a claim that the town held two men of the name: it is the ruling that nothing reached folds them, and the record is carried as it is printed, which is the state the cards are already in. `for_merge` is kept verbatim so the argument survives its refusal and a later anchor can reopen it. R3 named this shape and referred it to the owner; T-0844 rules it instead, because a ballot between two guesses on no evidence is not a decision the owner is better placed to make than the rule is, and tickets/README.md holds `blocked-owner` to rights, licensing, money and what the project is.
rules.C6: A MIDDLE INITIAL STANDING ALONE, OVER AN ANCHOR THE SAME SOURCE PRINTS WITH BOTH INITIALS. All four of: the lone token is a forename initial for NO bearer in the cluster; exactly one documented bearer of the surname carries it as a middle initial; the same source prints that man with both initials, so the loss the fold supposes is one the source itself demonstrates; and the printing the folded card was minted from is flagged uncertain by its own extraction. Written for T-0844's Temple row and deliberately too narrow to reach a stray middle initial anywhere else — drop any one of the four conditions and the card stays where it is. This is the rule T-0839 declined to invent, written with the guard it wanted.
rules.C7: ONE COMPOUND SURNAME, PRINTED SEVERAL WAYS, RULED AT THE PAGE. Two cards whose surnames differ only in a Dutch, French or German particle — Van Den against Van der, De against Du — where all four of: the forename initial agrees on every printing; the SAME publication is shown setting the particle more than one way for that initial and stem inside the window, so the variation is demonstrated rather than supposed; the whole corpus holds exactly ONE bearer of the stem at this town; and no source places two such people here at once. The demonstration is the load-bearing clause and it is what separates C7 from a resemblance: a merge across two printed surnames needs the printer's own inconsistency in evidence, not the reader's willingness to believe in it. Written for T-0842, whose ticket says the same thing in its own words — 'a merge across two printed surnames is a research ruling and needs a source, not a resemblance'.
rules.C8: A MIDDLE NAME IN FULL, STANDING ALONE, WHERE A SOURCE PRINTS THE SAME MAN BOTH WAYS. All four of: the folded card's whole printed forename is a DISTINCTIVE WORD — not an initial, and not a given name the corpus uses as one — that no bearer in the cluster carries as a forename; exactly one documented bearer of the surname carries that word as a MIDDLE NAME PRINTED IN FULL, so the fold is onto a name the town has actually read rather than onto an expansion this rule supplies; a source OUTSIDE the two cards prints that one man BOTH ways — with his forename, and with the middle name standing alone in the forename's place — so the loss the fold supposes is one a page demonstrates; and no source prints the two readings as separate entries, which is D3's discriminator and the thing that would make them two men. Written for T-0993's Blanchard row. It is C6's shape with the initial replaced by a word, and it leans on a different leg: C6's fourth condition is an extraction flagged uncertain, because an initial is one of twenty-six and needs the doubt; a distinctive middle name needs instead that some source be caught printing the man both ways, and that is what this rule asks for in its place. Drop any one of the four and the card stays where it is.
rules.C9: ONE SURNAME, TWO SPELLINGS OF ITS ENDING, DEMONSTRATED IN ONE COLUMN. C7's shape for a surname whose variation is not a Dutch or French particle but a letter of the name itself. All four of: the forename and the middle initial agree on every printing, so nothing but the spelling of the surname stands between the cards; the SAME publication is caught setting both spellings for that one man inside the window — on one page, and better on one page-run — so the variation is the printer's and is demonstrated rather than supposed; the whole corpus holds exactly ONE bearer of that forename-and-middle-initial at this town, and no source places two such people here at once; and the folded card carries no fact the survivor's record contradicts. The demonstration is the load-bearing clause, exactly as it is in C7: a merge across two printed surnames needs the printer's own inconsistency in evidence, not a reader's willingness to believe in it. A ONE-LETTER RESEMBLANCE IS NEVER ENOUGH ON ITS OWN, and T-1001 measured what it would cost if it were: turned into a mechanical fold over the land register's 427 named purchaser spellings, admitting one letter gathers a new rival for 200 of them and changes the shape of 42 proposals, 18 of which are already ruled by hand — tools/measure_surname_fold.py prints the table. That is why this rule asks for a page and not for a resemblance, and why it is applied one cluster at a time.
rules.C10: ONE FORENAME, TWO SPELLINGS OF IT, DEMONSTRATED IN ONE TITLE. C9's shape moved from the surname to the forename, and drawn to the same four conditions. All four of: the SURNAME agrees letter for letter and every middle initial agrees on every printing, so nothing but the spelling of the forename stands between the cards; the SAME publication is caught setting both spellings for that one man inside the window, so the variation is the printer's and is demonstrated rather than supposed; the whole corpus holds exactly ONE bearer of that surname-and-middle-initial at this town, and no source places two such people here at once; and the folded card carries no fact the survivor's record contradicts. The demonstration is the load-bearing clause, exactly as it is in C7 and C9 — a merge across two printed forenames needs the printer's own inconsistency in evidence, not a reader's willingness to believe in it. Written for T-1002's Heacock row. A ONE-LETTER RESEMBLANCE IS NEVER ENOUGH ON ITS OWN and this rule is not a licence to fold on distance: tools/measure_card_fuzzy_candidates.py puts one letter of slack over the town's own cards and it proposes 71 pairs the exact test does not, among them John Hale against John Vale, Mark Noble against Mary Noble and James Sheldon against James Wheldon. A distance cannot tell those from this one. That is why the rule asks for a page, and why it is applied one cluster at a time.
rules.C11: TWO SPELLINGS DISCHARGING ONE DOCUMENTED OFFICE, WITH A NON-NAME DISCRIMINATOR. The shape C10 cannot reach: two spellings of one forename that NO single title is caught setting both ways, where the printings are nevertheless tied together by an office the town's own record holds. All four of: the surname agrees letter for letter and the middle initial or middle name agrees, so nothing but the forename's spelling separates the cards; BOTH spellings are printed in the discharge of ONE seat that only one person can hold at a time, so a second bearer is not merely unattested but impossible against the record; an INDEPENDENT NON-NAME DISCRIMINATOR ties the two printings to that one seat — a vote tally, a term of office, a signature on an instrument — and not the name, which is the thing in dispute; and the folded card carries no fact the survivor's record contradicts. Written for T-1002's Beaubien row, where the discriminator is an election return: two histories print the same five names and the same five vote tallies for the town's first board of trustees and spell the third man's forename two ways, and the town's own ordinance then names four of those five, under the second spelling, as the committee the board appointed. THE OFFICE IS THE LOAD-BEARING CLAUSE and it is narrower than a trade or an address: a trade two men can share and a street two men can live on, so neither would satisfy this rule. Drop any one of the four conditions and the card stays where it is.
rules.C12: TWO SPELLINGS ON ONE CLOSED ROLL, RESOLVED BY EXHAUSTION OVER THE ROLL. The shape C10 and C11 both leave standing: two spellings of one forename that no single title is caught setting both ways for one man, and that no single seat is caught holding both — where a CLOSED ROLL nevertheless leaves the survivor exactly one entry he can be. All four of: the surname agrees letter for letter and no middle initial or middle name DISAGREES on any printing of either card; a CLOSED ROLL inside the window — a list the document itself bounds and enumerates — does NOT print the survivor's spelling while an INDEPENDENT NON-NAME FACT puts him on it, the roll being the poll of the election that returned him, or the register of a body he is documented to have belonged to; EVERY OTHER bearer of the surname on that roll is accounted for by a card of its own that the survivor is not, so the folded spelling is the only entry left for him, and the exhaustion is WORKED OVER THE WHOLE ROLL AND PRINTED rather than asserted; and no source reached prints the two spellings as separate entries, which is D3's discriminator, while the folded card carries no fact the survivor's record contradicts. THE EXHAUSTION IS THE LOAD-BEARING CLAUSE, and it is what makes this a count and not a resemblance: the rule never weighs how alike the two spellings are and would fire the same way on two that look nothing alike — which is the only reason it may be applied at three letters of difference, where C9 and C10 are held to one. Written for T-1026's Medard row, where the roll is the thirty-name poll of 10 August 1833. IT IS NARROWER THAN IT READS. A roll whose membership the document does not bound — a newspaper's prose, a subscription list, a trade's advertisers, a directory — is NOT a closed roll and cannot be exhausted, because absence from it means nothing; and a roll that does not itself state the ground on which the survivor must appear cannot supply the second condition, since 'he ought to be here somewhere' is the reader's expectation and not the document's. Drop any one of the four and the card stays where it is.
rules.D5: ONE CLOSED ROLL ENTERS BOTH SPELLINGS, SIDE BY SIDE. The exact converse of C12's exhaustion, and the refusal C9 needs when the page it asks for turns up and says the opposite. All three of: a CLOSED ROLL inside the window — a list the document itself bounds and enumerates — prints BOTH spellings as SEPARATE ENTRIES; the roll is one that enters a person ONCE, so a second entry is the document's own count and not its hand wavering; and no other source is caught setting the two spellings for one man. Where C9 folds on a printer caught varying, this refuses on a clerk caught distinguishing: the same instrument that would have demonstrated the variation demonstrates the opposite, and it outranks any resemblance between the two strings. A ROLL OF TRANSACTIONS IS NOT SUCH A ROLL and cannot fire this rule — the land register enters one buyer once per parcel and one man 47 times, so two spellings inside one week there are the clerk's hand, which is why the Pearson cluster below folds on the same kind of evidence this one stands on. Written for T-1132's David/Davis row, where the roll is the 115-name tax list of the Town of Chicago for 1833 and the two entries are its numbers 23 and 24.
rules.D6: TWO RETURNS OF ONE SERIAL ROLL, AND NEITHER OF THEM SETS BOTH SPELLINGS. The refusal for a pair whose ONLY witness is a SERIAL closed roll — a list one office re-compiles and re-publishes on a schedule, the Chicago post office's returns of letters uncalled-for being this corpus's one example of the shape. All four of: neither card is an anchor, so anchored() finds no trade, no dwelling and no research behind either; every appearance either card carries stands on that roll and on nothing else, so there is no second body of evidence to ask; NO SINGLE return sets both spellings, which is C9's demonstration absent; and the two spellings stand on returns the office closed on different days, so the roll never had the occasion to enter one man twice and D5's counter-demonstration is absent with it. Where C9 folds on a printer caught varying and D5 refuses on a clerk caught distinguishing, D6 rules the case where the instrument was never asked the question: the roll is serial, so its silence is neither evidence for the fold nor against it, and a one-letter distance is all that would be left to fold on — which is what T-1001 measured over the land register's 427 purchaser spellings and refused. It is D4's answer in another domain: the cards stay two because nothing reached joins them, and that is NOT a claim that the town held two men of the name. `for_merge` is kept verbatim so the argument survives its refusal. TWO THINGS DEFEAT IT, and both are live. If one return is shown to set both spellings the ruling becomes C9's or D5's. And if the two cards prove to stand on ONE PRINTED LINE of one return, read two ways by two impressions of it, then they were never two printings at all and C9 fires at its strongest — which is what happened to Fraser/Frazer and Vandine/Vandino in the same pass that wrote this rule, and it is why the return a card stands on is checked before D6 is reached for. Written for T-1133.
rules.C13: THE COLUMN'S OWN ALPHABET NAMES THE LETTER THE READING LOST. Not a printer varying and not a clerk distinguishing, but THIS PROJECT'S OWN EXTRACTION dropping or mangling a surname's first letter, where the source is an ALPHABETISED list and the list's own order says what the letter was. All five of: the disputed reading comes from a list the document sets in alphabetical sections, and the section it stands in is demonstrated by the entries above and below it in that same run rather than assumed; the reading's surname begins with a letter that is NOT that section's, and the deviation is at the FIRST letter — where a broken capital, a rule, an ampersand or a section mark is what a scan turns into a letter; restoring the section's letter yields a surname the town already holds under the SAME forename; the rejected spelling occurs NOWHERE in the whole deposited corpus, so it is not a name anybody is shown setting; and the folded card carries no fact the survivor's record contradicts. THE ALPHABET IS THE LOAD-BEARING CLAUSE, and it is evidence of the same kind C9 asks for — the document demonstrating the variation rather than the reader supposing it — moved from the printer's inconsistency to the compositor's order. Written for T-1134's Anight/Knight row, where the letter list of 30 June 1835 sets '& Anight, Clark' inside the K run of its F-to-L alphabet, between 'Kirne, E. Capt.' and 'King, Neheminh'. The extraction pass that read that column ANTICIPATED this rule and refused to do its work: its own note says a name whose initial disagrees with its section 'is a MISREADING, not a clipping, and stands as printed — correcting it would be a guess, and identity.json is the only place two spellings may become one person.' This is that place. IT IS NARROW. It reaches the first letter of a surname on an alphabetised list and nothing else: a list with no sections cannot fire it, a deviation in the middle of a name cannot fire it, and a restored letter that lands on no existing card of the same forename cannot fire it — that is a reading to file, not a fold.
rules.D7: C9'S SHAPE, AND THE PAGE C9 ASKS FOR DOES NOT EXIST. The standing refusal for two cards one letter apart in the surname and identical in the forename where every other condition of C9 is met — one bearer of the forename on each side, nothing contradicted, often a stem so rare the town holds nothing else like it — and NO title reached is caught setting both spellings for one man. All three of: the pair would satisfy C9 but for its demonstration; the whole deposited corpus has been SEARCHED for both spellings and what the search returned is printed in the refusal, including when it returned nothing; and the two bodies of evidence do not touch, each spelling standing on sources the other's never sets. This is NOT a claim that the town held two men of the name. It is the ruling that nothing reached folds them, and it is what T-1130 asked for in its own words: 'C9's load-bearing clause is a page that demonstrates the variation, and a pair with no such page is refused and says so.' `for_merge` is kept verbatim so the argument survives its refusal and a later page reopens it. WHY A RULE AND NOT A SHRUG: T-1001 measured the alternative. A blanket one-letter fold over the land register's 427 purchaser spellings gathers a new rival for 200 of them and turns 24 named matches into losses; tools/measure_surname_fold.py prints the table. Refusing on the missing page is the only thing standing between this project and that measurement. D6 AND THIS RULE WERE WRITTEN THE SAME NIGHT, BY THE TWO HALVES OF ONE TICKET, AND THE NUMBERING IS THE ONLY THING THAT SEPARATES THEM IN TIME. T-1133's D6 is the SPECIAL CASE: a pair whose only witness is a SERIAL closed roll — the post office's returns of letters uncalled-for — where no single return sets both spellings and the two stand on returns closed on different days, so the instrument was never asked the question. D7 is the GENERAL one, and it is what the town's own lists need: the two spellings stand on different INSTRUMENTS entirely — a tax roll against a newspaper, a poll book against a directory — so there is no single roll whose silence could be weighed either way. Reach for D6 first where both cards are letter-list cards; D7 is the rest. Both refuse for one reason and it is the same reason: C9 asks for a page and there is no page.
rules.C14: TWO SPELLINGS OF ONE SURNAME ON A CLOSED ROLL, RESOLVED BY EXHAUSTION OVER THE ROLL. C12's shape with its two halves swapped — there the surname agrees and the forename varies, here the forename agrees and the surname varies — and it is written because C12 as drafted reaches a forename only. All four of: THE FORENAME AGREES LETTER FOR LETTER and no middle initial or middle name disagrees on any printing of either card, so nothing but the spelling of the surname stands between the cards, which is C9's first condition and this rule fires only where C9's DEMONSTRATION is the thing that is missing; a CLOSED ROLL inside the window — a list the document itself bounds and enumerates — does NOT print the survivor's spelling while an INDEPENDENT NON-NAME FACT puts him on it, and the fact is one the project's own committed record RE-DERIVES rather than one a reader supplies; EVERY OTHER ENTRY on that roll prints a name the survivor cannot be, so the folded entry is the only one left for him, and the exhaustion is WORKED OVER THE WHOLE ROLL AND PRINTED rather than asserted; and no source reached prints the two spellings as SEPARATE ENTRIES, which is D5's discriminator and D3's, while the folded card carries no fact the survivor's record contradicts. THIS RULE IS D7'S ANSWER, AND D7 IS WHERE THE PAIR OTHERWISE LANDS. D7, written the night before this one, is the standing REFUSAL for exactly this shape: one letter of surname, an identical forename, the whole corpus searched, and the two spellings standing on instruments that never touch — 'a tax roll against a newspaper' in its own words, which is this pair precisely. D7 refuses because nothing reached folds them. C14 is what fires when something does, and it is NOT a page: D7 says 'a later page reopens it' and no page has turned up or is claimed. What reopens it here is a COUNT, and the count is admissible where a page is not because it never weighs how alike the two strings are. REACH FOR D7 FIRST. C14 requires a closed roll AND a re-derivable fact putting the survivor on it; a pair with neither — which is most of them — is D7's, and this rule must never be read as softening that refusal. THE EXHAUSTION IS THE LOAD-BEARING CLAUSE, exactly as in C12. TWO THINGS ARE DIFFERENT FROM C12 AND BOTH ARE HARDER. First, the count is run over the WHOLE ROLL and not over a surname bucket: the varying half here is the surname, so 'every other bearer of the surname' is not a set the roll can be asked for, and a count over the bearers of the FORENAME cannot close either, because a roll of this kind prints entries with no forename at all — thirteen of the 115 on the one this rule was written for. Second, the exclusion is orthographic where C12's is by card, and that is the direction T-1001 permits: this rule never FOLDS on a one-letter resemblance, it EXCLUDES on a many-letter difference, and saying that 'Beaubien' is not a printing of 'Pruyne' asks nothing of a reader's willingness to believe. It is still held to a gap: the entries the roll prints must leave the disputed one ALONE at one letter with clear air behind it, and a second entry arriving anywhere in that gap reopens the ruling. THE SECOND CONDITION IS THE ONE THAT NEARLY REFUSED THIS, and it is where the rule is narrower than it reads. 'He owned ground in the town, so the town's property roll must carry him' is admissible only when the ground is shown to be INSIDE the line and the showing is geometry the gate re-derives. The argument one step weaker — he bought at the town's own auction, so he is the kind of man the roll carries — is T-1017's, and T-1017 MEASURED it and refused it: at that sale thirteen of 105 buyers carry a surname the layer holds nobody of, upheld matches are a minority of its buyers, and the sale prints twenty surnames more than one way, PRUYNE among them. A rule that admitted the weaker form would be that refusal reversed by momentum. Written for T-1135, where the roll is the 115-name tax list of the Town of Chicago for 1833. Drop any one of the four and the card stays where it is.
rules.D8: C10'S SHAPE ON THE FORENAME, AND THE TITLE C10 ASKS FOR DOES NOT EXIST. D7's mirror, written for T-1291 because D7 reaches a SURNAME only and five of the one-letter pairs vary in the forename instead. All three of: the pair would satisfy C10 but for its demonstration — the surname agrees letter for letter, every middle initial agrees, so nothing but the spelling of the forename stands between the cards; the whole deposited corpus and the reading index have been SEARCHED for both spellings and what the search returned is printed in the refusal, including when it returned nothing; and NO single printing — one issue of one paper, one roll, one directory entry — is caught setting both spellings for one man. `for_merge` is kept verbatim so the argument survives its refusal and a later page reopens it, exactly as in D7. THIS IS NOT A CLAIM THAT THE TOWN HELD TWO PEOPLE OF THE NAME. It is the ruling that nothing reached folds them. Where the two forenames are not two spellings of one name at all — Mark against Mary, Byram against Hyram — the refusal is stronger than D8 and the `against_merge` says so.
rules.D9: A SHARED SOURCE ID IS NOT A SHARED PRINTING. The refusal for a pair whose two spellings sit under ONE source id where that id names a CORPUS and not a printing, and no single printing inside it sets both. Two of this project's source ids are corpora: `chicago_newspapers_1833_1835` is three years of two papers, and `chicago_voter_lists_1833_1835_irad` is FOUR separate closed rolls — the poll of 10 August 1833, the tax list of 1833, the poll filed 11 August 1834 and the 1835 poll — bundled into one transcription. C9 and C10 ask for one publication CAUGHT setting both spellings for one man; a shared corpus id is not that catch, and neither is a grep that finds both spellings somewhere in one file. All four of: the pair would satisfy C9 or C10 but for its demonstration; both readings cite ONE source id, so D6's and D7's 'the two bodies of evidence do not touch' is literally false and neither refusal is available as written; the printings are IDENTIFIED — issue and column, or roll and entry — and NO single one of them sets both spellings; and no single roll enters both spellings as separate entries either, which is D5's discriminator and would refuse harder. WHY THIS RULE HAD TO BE WRITTEN: without it a pair like Foot/Foote, whose two spellings stand on two different rolls of one transcription, falls through the gap between C9's missing demonstration and D7's non-touching instruments and reads as unrulable. It is not unrulable; it is refused, for D7's reason, measured at the ROLL instead of at the source id. The unit C9 reasons about is the PRINTING, and this rule is nothing but that sentence applied. `for_merge` is kept verbatim.
rules.D10: THE NAMES DISAGREE BEYOND THE ONE LETTER. A pair the one-letter test joins whose FORENAMES also fail to agree: two different middle initials both printed, a middle initial against a middle NAME, two different given names, or an honorific that fixes a different person. C9's and C10's FIRST condition — that nothing but the one spelling stands between the cards — is unmet, so neither rule is reachable, and D7 and D8 do not apply either because they exist for pairs that fail only the DEMONSTRATION. Refused on the names, before any question of a page. This is the least interesting shape in the one-letter pool and it is why the pool is not a worklist: a distance measured over a whole name cannot tell 'one letter of surname' from 'one letter of surname plus a different man's forename'. Where neither card is documented beyond a list and the disagreement is two printed middle initials, R3 is the narrower rule and is used instead — the `barry-j` cluster is its precedent.
rules.U2: AMBIGUOUS, AND THAT IS THE FINISHED ANSWER. The owner, 2026-09-17, on T-1290 and T-1291: the research spend is a CHECK before reconstruction, not a programme — 'a pair that cannot be ruled on the evidence is recorded as ambiguous, with both readings kept, and that is a finished answer, not a deferral and not a new ticket'. U1 files a question and names a ticket that owns it; U2 states that the evidence does not decide, keeps both readings, and files NOTHING. It is a refusal in the project's own sense — the project already prefers a refusal to an invention — and the gate treats it as U1 does, because the gate asks that a cluster be WEIGHED and not that it be merged. A U2 ruling still carries `for_merge` and `against_merge`: what it drops is the promise that somebody will come back.

rulings.for: The owner's own demonstration in T-0839. Four cards, one man: Lieut. James Allen of the United States Army, the harbour engineer. hh_allen_lieut_james is the only card that knows his trade (army_officer, from the Democrat of 13 August 1834, column 2) and the only one the ladder never reached; hh_allen_james is the one the ladder graded best and it knows nothing about the army. 'Lieut Allen', 'Lieut J Allen' and 'Lieut. James Allen' are the same title, the same initial and the same full name, printed by the Democrat and the American between March 1834 and July 1835; 'James Allen' is that full name without the rank. Merged he is one attested man with a trade, four sources and two newspapers behind him.
rulings.against: Nothing reached says the town held a second James Allen. Two other Allens are on cards and both are ruled distinct below on their own forenames.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the card that carries the TRADE, because the trade is the thing a merge onto any other card would lose: mint_civic_residents.py writes `occupation: none_recorded` onto every card it derives and would re-derive an army officer away.

rulings.for: THE CONTRADICTING MIDDLE INITIAL WAS NEVER PRINTED — IT IS A DIGIT. (T-0854, folded into T-0844 and ruled here.) chicago_democrat_1833_12_10#c012 transcribes the advertisement as 'TO LOAN, / JOHN 8. KINZIE, / [F]orwarding & Commission [MERCHANT] / CHICAGO—ILLINOIS', and the `as_printed` string the extraction records is 'JOHN 8. KINZIE'. `8` is a digit, and no compositor set a digit inside a personal name; the lines around it come off the same scan as 'WIBRORA TT' and '[uncertain: orwarding & Commission | Fi]', so the reading at this spot is demonstrably wrecked. 'John S. Kinzie' is the extractor's NORMALISATION of that digit and no witness supplies the S. This is the fourth instance of the digit-for-letter fault T-0721 holds — '8. G. Abbot', 'A. 8. Perry', 'James I1. Gabbs' — and the first that reached a card. WHAT IS LEFT ONCE THE S GOES is a card minted from one printing of 'John [unread]. Kinzie, forwarding and commission merchant, Chicago—Illinois'. Four Kinzie men stand on the town's cards — James, John H., Robert A. and this one — and John Harris Kinzie is the only bearer of the forename John. His own card's `works_at` is `jh_kinzie_forwarding_store`, from his own 1834 advertisement in the same paper: the trade printed beside the unread initial is his trade. That is C3, a bare forename onto an anchor, corroborated by the trade INDEPENDENTLY of the initials — the same corroboration T-0732 required, and cited, for the R. A. Kinzie merge in this cluster.
rulings.against: The Kinzie surname is the one T-0839 named as this project's trap, and T-0732 records a Kinzie mis-fold. The guard against repeating it is that nothing here rests on the surname: data/research/books/crosswalk.json's rule — nothing merged, linked or graded on a shared surname — governs, and this fold is made on the forename and the trade. The elder John Kinzie, dead in 1828, is held by no record in this project and is not a rival. T-0854 said the merge stayed the owner's call; T-0844 is the ticket that makes it, and tickets/README.md holds `blocked-owner` to rights, licensing, real money and what the project is — an initial nobody printed is not one of them.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the anchor: the north-division household with the forwarding store, Andreas, Wau-Bun and the voter rolls. T-0732 §Q1 predicted this line — 'Four Kinzie household cards now stand where the ticket counted six. The count could yet fall to three' — and it is three.

rulings.for: C6, ON A SIGNATURE LINE THE EXTRACTION ITSELF COULD NOT READ. `temple_t` is minted from one claim, chicago_democrat_1834_12_03#c022, whose quote runs '[uncertain: inieied Store, on SouhOBN T: TEMPLI]' and whose normalisation reads 'Also, a large and beautifully [fi]nished Store, on South [Water street.] T. TEMPLE. Chicago, Sept. 20, 1834.' What is advertised is a three-storey store house sixty feet in one dimension with a wharf attached, a small dwelling house of two rooms, and a finished store on South Water Street — river-frontage property, let by whoever owned it. The four conditions: (1) 'T.' is a forename initial for no Temple this town holds — the cards carry Dr John Taylor Temple and his brother Dr Peter Temple, and the press corpus's only other Temple is a '[Lew]is Temple' conjectured out of a letter list and minted onto no card; (2) exactly one documented Temple carries T as a middle initial, John Taylor Temple; (3) the same paper sets that man with both initials — 'J. T. Temple' eight times in this corpus and 'Dr. J. T. Temple' beside it — so 'J. T. TEMPLE' losing its first initial is a loss the source demonstrates rather than one this ruling supposes; (4) the printing is flagged uncertain by its own extraction. He is also the Temple the property records reach: he stands in the public-domain land tract sales, and three separate advertisements give his premises as the town's landmark at the corner of Lake and Franklin, one block off South Water.
rulings.against: A card whose only forename token is a MIDDLE initial has no rule in this project, and T-0839 refused to invent one because a loose rule would attach every stray middle initial in the corpus. C6 is written for that objection and states where it does not fire: drop any one of its four conditions and the card stays where it is. Dr Peter Temple is on the survivor's own household record and his initial is P, so he is not a rival for the T.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the anchor: physician, arrived early July 1833 with a wife and four children, Andreas and the Baptist history and the voter rolls and the land tract sales. `temple_t` carries one advertisement.

rulings.for: ONE ADVERTISEMENT, PRINTED IN BOTH PAPERS. `hunt_c_s` was minted from chicago_democrat_1835_08_12#c007 and `hunt_charles_cotesworth_pinckney` carries chicago_american_1835_08_29#c002, and the two claims are the SAME advertisement: a High School for Young Ladies proposed on a permanent foundation at Chicago, the first term commencing Monday 17 August, names to be left before that day at the office of Henry Moore, Esq. The Democrat sets the proprietor's name as 'Canes HUNT' and its extraction reads it 'Hunt, C[harle]s'; the American sets '[ARLES HUNT' and its extraction reads it 'Charles Hunt'. Rule C5: a bracketed forename is the transcriber naming the man, and it outranks any inference drawn from initials. Two hands, two copies, one schoolmaster called Charles Hunt.
rulings.and_the_s_is_not_a_middle_initial: `hunt_c_s` is named 'C S Hunt' because the mint split 'C[harle]s' into two tokens and took the trailing s of the abbreviation Chas. for a second initial. There is no S in the printing for anything to contradict, so T-0839's ground against this merge — 'the middle initial S contradicts C' — was argued on a token the source does not set. The same fault as the Kinzie row below, arrived at by a different route: a parse, not an OCR digit.
rulings.against: The full name Charles Cotesworth Pinckney Hunt is printed only by Fergus's old-settler death notice of 21 April 1892, forty-seven years after the scene year; the fold of that notice onto the American's 'Charles Hunt' was made before this pass and is not re-litigated here. The town's other Hunt card is Henry N. Hunt, whose forename is not Charles.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the card the town already reads — the American's printing and the death notice — and the folded card brings the Democrat's printing of the same advertisement. Both extractions record the occupation 'schoolmaster' and the survivor's occupation field still reads none_recorded; that is a spend for the pass that owns the occupation field, not a hand-edit here.

H. dentist, 133 Lake st. house same'. A trade, a premises, a street and a tenancy dated back to the summer of 1834: that is an anchor on this file's own definition, and T-0839's `against_merge` — 'neither card documents the man' — is wrong on the evidence its own card carries. `kennicott_w_l` is one line of the 1835 poll list, 'Kennicott, W. L.', and nothing else. The cluster holds exactly one documented bearer of the forename William, one card carries his full name, and the variation is confined to the middle initial on a manuscript list a copyist set — C4's shape exactly, the shape the owner ratified on Haddock.

H. and two from M. H., so the nearer reading is taken; the further one is recorded here rather than folded, because C4 attaches an initial to ONE documented bearer of the forename and M is not a bearer of William.

Norton` is the town's only ship-carpenter, arrived 16 November 1833, builder of the Dearborn Street drawbridge in March 1834. The initials agree letter for letter, N against Nelson and R against R, and he is the ONE full forename of this surname carrying N: the town's other Norton card is `Wm. H. Norton`, a W. That is C2 exactly, and identity_master.json has been deriving the same merge under M2 since it was written — id_norton_nelson_r holds both cards and names only the first as canonical, which is why the letter-list card never got a ladder rung at all (T-0692).
rulings.against: A letter list names a person whose mail is at Chicago and nothing more, so the folded card could in principle be a Norton the town does not otherwise hold. Nothing reached says so: no second N. Norton is printed anywhere in the corpus, and the card's own research pass (T-0483) closed `no_corroboration_yet` — it found no separate man, which is the outcome that makes the initial's one rival the only rival.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the card that carries the TRADE, the dated arrival and the structures-layer link (data/structures/dearborn_street_drawbridge.json names him as its builder). The letter-list card carries one appearance, and the merge brings it onto him as what it is: a letter waiting at the post office on 1 July 1835, the scene date, for a man the town already documents.

rulings.for_merge: Both are in the same paper, chicago_democrat_1833_1835, and Saunders is not a common surname in this town. Kept verbatim from T-0839 so the argument survives its refusal.
rulings.against_merge: THE ANCHOR EXISTS AND CANNOT REACH THE OTHER CARD'S DATE. William W. Saunders is documented: the Democrat of 18 March 1834 (c002) prints a Cook Circuit Court attachment notice naming him, 'William W. Saunders, formerly of Cook co. Ill.', over a dwelling house and tenement of his the sheriff had attached — a court record with a dwelling in it, so C4's anchor is present where T-0839 said no anchor was. But that same record calls him FORMERLY of the county in March 1834, and the only date `saunders_william_s` carries is a letter uncalled-for at the Chicago post office on 1 July 1835. Firing C4 would have the anchor absorb a line dated after the anchor's own record says he had gone. The middle initials S and W disagree, nothing else touches either man, and the cards stay two.
rulings.not_a_claim_that: This does not assert that the town held two Saunderses. It rules that nothing reached folds them. A source that puts one William Saunders at Chicago on both sides of March 1834 would reopen it.

rulings.against_merge: A WOMAN AND A MAN, AND THE PAGE PRINTS THE HONORIFIC. The Chicago Democrat of 19 August 1835 (c007) invites the town to a sale "at the hous[e] of Mrs. C. Taylor, Water-st." — she keeps a house and hosts the Juvenile Society in it. The rival card is Charles H. Taylor, Anson's brother on hh_taylor_anson: a carpenter on the 1833, 1834 and 1835 poll lists, in the federal land tract register and in the 1840 census, every one of them a man's record. Merging would assert that the notice named him, which no reading of "Mrs." supports. THE PROOF HERE IS NOT BROWN'S PROOF, and the difference is why this ruling is written out rather than cited: R6 and D3 were built on ONE SOURCE PRINTING BOTH READINGS as separate entries, because `Mrs. Rufus B. Brown` and `Brown, Rufus B.` are identical once the honorific is stripped and nothing in the letters tells a Rufus from an Eliza. These two are not identical after the strip — `Taylor, C.` against `Taylor, Charles H.` — so the pair never needed that proof to be held apart; what joins them is the ordinary initial rule (C2 on the card side, M2 in the derivation) reaching across an honorific it cannot see. That is the shape T-0951 now carries.
rulings.for_merge: Only the initial. Strip "Mrs." and `C.` expands to exactly one full Taylor forename in this town — Charles — with no rival, which is C2's own test and would ordinarily land the merge. It is also true that this is exactly how the period prints a married woman — the honorific standing on her husband's forename, whoever he was — so the shape itself argues nothing either way. That is an argument for a KINSHIP, not for one card: R6 (#998) settled that a wife is not her husband.
rulings.survivor_note: Neither card moves. No kin[] row is written either, and the absence is deliberate: no source names a wife of Charles H. Taylor in 1835, and hh_taylor_anson's own note already REFUSES the one candidate — data/structures/wolf_point_tavern.json's "Charles and Mary Taylor" of 1831-1833 — on the ground that at least four distinct Taylor men stand in these sources. Written up on hh_taylor_c under T-0960; the derivation still folds `person_taylor_mrs_c` onto `id_taylor_charles`, which is the finding T-0951 holds.

rulings.against: The Taylor surname holds Anson and William as well; neither begins with E.

rulings.for_merge: Both are Thompsons in the Democrat in the first quarter of 1834, and J expands to John.

rulings.for_merge: Both are Georges in chicago_democrat_1833_1835 and the town holds no third Walker of that forename. Kept verbatim from T-0839 so the argument survives its refusal.
rulings.against_merge: EACH MIDDLE INITIAL IS PRINTED TWICE, BY INDEPENDENT HANDS. George E. Walker is 'George E. Walker' in the Democrat's letter list of 2 July 1834 and 'Walker, George E.' in Fergus's old-settler death notice of 9 November 1874. George H. Walker is 'WALKER, GEORGE H' on the 1832 Black Hawk enrollment roll and 'G. H. Walker' in the Democrat's letter list of 1 April 1834. A copyist's mis-set is the WHOLE ground for folding a contradicted middle initial, and it does not survive two independent attestations on each side: four printings, two sources apiece, E twice and H twice. The town's other Walker cards are James and Jeremiah. T-0480's research adds, without asserting it, a George E. Walker in an 1835 Illinois land record near Utica — competing geography, recorded and not leaned on.
rulings.not_a_claim_that: This does not assert that the town held two George Walkers. It rules that the printings do not fold: the mis-set the merge would need is contradicted by the second attestation on each side.

rulings.for: THE PAGE THE TICKET ASKED FOR, READ — and it answers more than it was asked. The Chicago Democrat of 4 February 1834 (page 3, column 2, transcription lines 2092-2148) prints the officers the Chicago Temperance Society chose at its annual meeting in the Presbyterian Church on Thursday 30 January 1834, and its executive committee reads '[M]r. H. Vax Den Bocart' — normalized by the reading pass as H. Van Den Bogart. That is the printing this ruling was owed. THREE THINGS CAME WITH IT. (1) THE SAME PAPER SETS THE PARTICLE THREE WAYS. Searching the whole deposited Democrat run for the stem finds a THIRD Chicago printing nobody had extracted: the issue of 29 October 1834 (page 2, column 2, transcription line 970) carries 'H. Ven De Bogart' in the committee of seventy the anti-gambling town meeting appointed under J. H. Kinzie, standing among Whittier, Mosely, Fullerton, Beaubien, Saxton, Clybourn, Aaron Russell and J. S. Wright. So within sixteen months the Chicago Democrat sets this one man's particle as 'Van Den', 'Ven De' and — in the letter list of 20 May 1835 — 'Vanderbogart'. The DEN/DER difference the undecided ruling turned on is a difference the printer himself does not hold to, and it cannot be asked to separate two men. (2) THE STEM HAS ONE BEARER HERE. The newspapers' gazetteer carries exactly two Bogart-stem persons, person_h_van_den_bogart and person_h_vanderbogart, and both are forename initial H.; the only other occurrence of the stem in the whole 1833-1835 corpus is JAMES BOGERT, Jr., a director of an Oswego, New York vessel-insurance company printed in the Democrat's advertising columns of 17 June 1835, who is not a resident and is not an H. (3) THE HONORIFIC IS NOT DECIDED AGAINST THE DOCTOR. The column's left edge is clipped by one to four characters on almost every line of that notice ('[Ann]ual Mee[t]ing', '[C]apt. D. Wilcox', '[Li]eut. J. L. Thompson', '[Mr]. D. Harmon'), and the Bogart line survives as 'r.' with exactly one character lost — which 'Dr.' fits as exactly as the 'Mr.' the transcriber supplied. The two physicians on the same list, Dr John T. Temple as president and Dr Josiah C. Goodhue as vice-president, keep their 'Dr.' because their lines were not clipped. This is NOT read as an attestation that the committee man was a doctor; it is the narrower and sufficient point that the printing does not say he was not, so the honorific cannot be held against the fold. AND THE DATES BRACKET RATHER THAN CONTRADICT. Fergus's old-settler death notices print Dr Henry Van der Bogart twice (fdn0049, fdn0683) as dying at Naperville, Illinois on 8 April 1835; the letter 'Vanderbogart, H.' was advertised uncalled-for at the Chicago post office on 20 May 1835. A letter that goes uncalled-for six weeks after the man it was addressed to died is what these lists are for, and the deferral's own worry — recorded when this cluster was sent to T-0950 — resolves in favour of the fold rather than against it.
rulings.against: The particle is the whole of it, and it is now answered by the printer's own practice rather than by resemblance. What remains genuinely unproved is narrower and is stated here rather than buried: no single source prints two of these three readings side by side, so the fold rests on the corpus holding one bearer of the stem and not on one page naming the same man twice. Were a second H. Bogart of any particle to be read at Chicago in this window, this ruling is the thing to reopen.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is vanderbogart_henry, the only card that carries the FULL forename and the death notices behind it. The two folded cards each carry one press appearance and an initial: vanderbogart_h is the letter-list mint of the 20 May 1835 return, which vanderbogart_henry already cites at the same locator (chicago_democrat_1835_05_20#c013, record person_h_vanderbogart) — the plainest duplicate in the cluster, two cards on one printed line — and vandenbogart_h is the 4 February 1834 Temperance notice, which no other card holds and which the survivor gains by the fold.
rulings.note: T-0842 owned the question and T-0950 was folded into it; both are answered here, one ruling on three cards. L220 recorded the cost of leaving it open — the town reading 490 where 489 stood — and that cost is now paid rather than carried.

clusters.why_not_derived: THE CANDIDATE TEST CANNOT SEE THIS PAIR, AND THAT IS THE FINDING UNDER IT. `compatible()` weighs the FIRST forename token of each card — a full word against the same word, or an initial the word begins with — so `gantry` against `f gantry` is two different words and the two cards never fall into one bucket. Every duplicate this project has folded so far was one the derivation raised; this one was found by hand, by T-0990 reading the land register, and it is written into this file as a cluster of its own so the ruling is read by the same machinery. Widening `compatible()` to reach it is NOT done here: a rule that matches any forename token against any other would put every man's middle name in a bucket with every other man's first, and the cluster list is a worklist somebody has to read.

rulings.for: C7, AND THE TOWN'S OWN DIRECTORY PRINTS THE NAME WHOLE. Fergus 1843 has 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells [died, Brooklyn, N.Y., 1872.]' — forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey — and Fergus 1839 and Norris 1844 print the same man 'Francis G.' So the token the town carries as `Gantry` is that middle name, and the two cards are one word apart. The four conditions: (1) `Gantry` is a whole word and no Blanchard in the cluster carries it as a forename — the layer holds F Gantry Blanchard, W. G. Blanchard and, in the directories only, Joseph Blanchard the blacksmith; (2) exactly one documented bearer carries `Gantry` as a middle name printed in full, `blanchard_f_gantry`, whom the poll of 1834 prints 'Blanchard, F. Gantry' and Fergus 1843 prints out in full — W. G. Blanchard carries only the INITIAL G and never the word, so he is not a second bearer of it; (3) a source outside both cards prints this one man both ways, at one sale, in one week: the Illinois State Archives' public-domain land tract register enters the school section — section 16, T39N R14E, type SC — as 'BLANCHARD F G' and 'BLANCHARD F G AS' on 22 October 1833 (purchase nos 0376893-0376895, volume 818 page 010) and as 'BLANCHARD GURTREY' on 22 and 24 October 1833 (purchase nos 0367525-0367530, volume 817 page 027). A clerk dropping the forename and setting this man's middle name alone is therefore a thing the record does, not a thing this ruling supposes; (4) no source prints the two readings as separate entries. The two cards stand on two different lists of one volume — tax_1833 entry 5 'Blanchard, Gantry', poll_1834 entry 13 'Blanchard, F. Gantry' — and each list holds exactly ONE Blanchard. D3's discriminator is a source printing both, and no source does. WHAT THE MERGE GAINS: the arrival bound moves from 1834-12-31 back to 1833-12-31 on the tax list's own evidence, and the town stops holding a `projected_resident` who is in fact its best-documented Blanchard.
rulings.against: The two readings are genuinely separate readings and not one extraction read twice — different lists, different years, different lines of data/research/civic/records/voter_lists_1833_1835.json — so the case is not the easy one where a duplicate is a transcription artefact. Against that: a tax list of 1833 and a poll list of 1834 are exactly the pair a man appears on twice, and appearing on both is the ordinary case, not the suspicious one. The one thing that would say two men is a father and a son sharing the surname, one printed Gantry and one F. Gantry; nothing reached prints a second Gurtrey Blanchard anywhere — not the directories of 1839, 1843 or 1844, not the press corpus, not the church registers, not the land register, whose four spellings of the surname are all readings of this one name. W. G. Blanchard is the layer's other documented Blanchard and his forename initial is W, which is not F and is not Gantry; he stands, and is ruled distinct below.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the card the DIRECTORIES reach. `blanchard_f_gantry` carries five sources, the 1839 and 1844 later-trade and later-address blocks, and the land register's rows; `blanchard_gantry` carries one line of the tax list of 1833. Both are civic mints, so the fold lands through the crosswalk and mint_civic_residents.py re-spends the joined identity — nothing here is written onto the card by hand.

rulings.against_merge: W. G. Blanchard is a house-and-land agent the Chicago Democrat names on 9 July 1834, and his forename initial is W. Francis Gurtrey Blanchard's is F. Two explicit and different forename initials on two documented men is D1, and the register's own crosswalk refuses W. G. against every Blanchard reading it holds on the same ground.
rulings.for_merge: The surname, the middle initial G, and a trade that would suit either man: a house-and-land agent of 1834 and a real-estate dealer of 1839 are the same business. That is a coincidence of trade in a town where land was the trade, and it moves nothing against two different forename initials.

clusters.why_not_derived: THE CANDIDATE TEST BUCKETS BY SURNAME AND FOLDS THE SURNAME EXACTLY. `clusters()` in tools/consolidate_town_cards.py groups the town's cards by `forename_tokens()[0]`, so `kimberley` and `kimberly` are two buckets and the two cards never meet, however well their forenames agree. The same exact fold is in `tools/namesake.py`, which is how the pair was found: T-0990 cohort B is DEFINED by `rivals[]` being empty, and the land register's KIMBERLEY EDMUND S came back with no rival while the layer held the closest namesake it could have. An empty `rivals[]` means 'no namesake of that spelling', not 'no namesake'. Widening either fold is NOT done here and T-1001 measured why: see C9, and tools/measure_surname_fold.py. The cluster is written into this file by hand so the ruling is read by the same machinery as every other.

rulings.for: ONE COLUMN OF ONE ISSUE SETS THE NAME BOTH WAYS, AND THE TOWN HAS ALREADY RULED ON HALF OF IT. (1) The demonstration. The Chicago Democrat of 1 July 1835, printed page 3, column 2, carries two claims about the same week's meetings: at lines 2660-2677 (claim c010) the signature block of the committee that invited the Secretary of War to a public dinner, which prints 'E. S. Kimberly'; and at lines 2721-2801 (claim c011) the report of the Democratic Republican meeting held at the Eagle Coffee House on 29 June, which prints 'E. S. Kimberley' among the committee of fourteen and then, four sentences later in the same article, 'on the motion of Dr. Kimberly was excused'. One issue, one page, one column, one week — and the surname set three ways. The variation is the compositor's, and this is the page that shows it. (2) The town has already ruled the FIRST of those two readings. `kimberly_e_s`, minted from c010, was folded onto `kimberly_edmund_s` in T-0839 under C0, on the owner's own instruction. `kimberley_ed` is minted from c011. So this project has already said that the E. S. Kimberly of that column is Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly; what is ruled here is the same initials in the next article of the same column. (3) The forename and the middle initial agree on every printing reached: 'E. S. Kimberley' (Democrat, 1 July 1835), 'Ed. Kimberley' (1840 federal census, printed page 234 line 3), 'Edmund S. Kimberly' (Democrat, 1833-1834), 'Kimberly, Dr. E. S.' (poll list of 1834), 'Kimberly, Dr. Edmund S.' (Fergus 1839) and 'Kimberly, Edmund Stoughten, physician, 101 Lake' (Fergus 1843). Nothing but the surname's ending separates them. (4) One bearer. The town's other Kimberlys are Ira and Osa, and 'Edmund L.' — already folded onto this man in T-0839 as the S read as an L. None is an Edmund S., and none is a physician. The Democrat of 26 November 1833 prints 'Dr. Kimberlie, Secretary' of a meeting of the citizens of Cook county, a third spelling of the same doctor in the same office his card records, and the corpus holds no second Edmund Kimberl(e)y at this town in any of the three. (5) It is not one transcriber wandering, either: the Illinois State Archives' public-domain tract register enters KIMBERLEY EDMUND S, and the 1840 census sheet reads Ed. Kimberley — two bodies of record independent of the Democrat spelling the ending the same way.
rulings.against: The two cards were minted from GENUINELY DIFFERENT readings — c010 and c011 are two claims with their own locators, and the 1840 census head is a third document — so this is not the easy case where a duplicate is one extraction read twice. Against that: two claims in one column of one issue are exactly where a compositor's spelling wanders, and the article itself is caught wandering inside its own paragraph. The one thing that would say two men is a second Edmund S. Kimberl(e)y at Chicago, and nothing reached prints one: not Andreas, not the history of medicine at Chicago, not Fergus 1839 or 1843, not Norris 1844, not the tax list of 1833 or the poll of 1834, not the press corpus, and not the land register, whose only Kimberley rows are Edmund S. and Ira. NOTHING IS PROMOTED TO MAKE THIS TIDY, AND ONE THING IS LOST. The survivor's grade — attested, G1a, off Andreas and the history of medicine — is exactly what it was before this ruling, and no 1840 household is back-projected. What the merge COSTS is the 1840 census head: `tools/crosswalk_census_1840_heads.py` gathers its 1835 bearers by surname and folds the surname exactly, the same fault this ticket found in the land crosswalk, so with `kimberley_ed` folded away the head 'Ed. Kimberley' (33S7-9YYJ-99F, printed page 234 line 3) falls from L7 CANDIDATE to L2 no_surname_in_the_1835_pools. That costs the town nothing it had ASSERTED — an L7 candidate asserts no identity, and its own reason said 'nothing independent of the name was found' — but it is a reading the domain can no longer reach, and it is written down here rather than left to be discovered. It is not repaired in this ruling on purpose: teaching that crosswalk the merge would hand its ladder the independent discriminator L6 asks for (Fergus 1843 prints 'Kimberly, Edmund Stoughten, physician, 101 Lake' and it is adjudicated to this person), and the head would come back MATCHED rather than as the candidate it was. A merge must not promote an identity as a side effect, so that is a research question of its own and is filed as its own ticket.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is `kimberly_edmund_s`, hand-authored and a PARTNER in hh_pruyne_kimberly rather than a head — the same shape as T-0839's Kimberly row, so the merge lands on the person and Peter Pruyne's record is untouched. What the folded card carries that the survivor did not: the Democrat's c011 reading, the 1840 census head, and the land register's KIMBERLEY EDMUND S rows. The first arrives through the card-merge crosswalk with the folded card's sources; what became of the second is in `against` above, and it is a loss, not a carry. The third is a purchaser spelling and needed its own amendment, because the land crosswalk gathers candidates by surname and after this merge the layer holds no Kimberley at all: data/research/land_sales/resident_rulings.json's KIMBERLEY EDMUND S ruling is re-pointed onto this survivor under T-1001, and tools/read_land_sales.py reads the landed card-merge adjudication so the surname the register prints still gathers the man the project has ruled it names. A ruling the derivation reads, not a special case beside it.

clusters.why_not_derived: THE CANDIDATE TEST WEIGHS THE FORENAME AS A STRING, AND MADORE IS NOT MEDORE. `compatible()` in tools/consolidate_town_cards.py admits a full forename against the same word, an initial the word begins with, or a card that prints a title and no forename at all. `madore` against `medore` is none of those three, so the two cards fell into the `beaubien` bucket together — the surname is one string — and then into two different clusters inside it, and the pair was never put to T-0839, T-0844 or T-0993. Not refused, not deferred, NEVER PROPOSED, which is the finding T-1002 is about. It was found by hand, by T-0961 ruling Moses and Kirkland's LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830 against the layer. Widening `compatible()` is NOT done here and the cost is measured: tools/measure_card_fuzzy_candidates.py.

rulings.for: ONE SEAT ON THE TOWN'S FIRST BOARD OF TRUSTEES, AND AN ELECTION RETURN THAT AGREES NUMBER FOR NUMBER UNDER BOTH SPELLINGS. (1) THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE TALLY, NOT THE NAME. Andreas prints the return of 10 August 1833 — 'The following were elected Trustees: T. J. V. Owen, 26 votes; George W. Dole, 26 votes; Madore B. Beaubien, 23 votes; John Miller, 20 votes; E. S. Kimberly, 20 votes' (data/research/civic/claims/town_findings_andreas_v1.json c003, and it is the claim hh_beaubien_madore.json's own note rests on). Moses and Kirkland print the same return in the same order — 'V. Owen, receiving 20 votes; George W. Dole the same; Medore B. Beaubien, 23, John Miller, 20, and E. S. Kirnberly, 20' (the r-n is the OCR's m) — at printed page 91 of volume 1, line 12340 of data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt. THE TWO PRINTINGS DO NOT AGREE THROUGHOUT and the disagreement is stated rather than hidden: Andreas gives Owen and Dole 26 votes each and Moses and Kirkland give them 20, so one of the two histories is wrong about the head of its own return. What they agree on exactly is the FIVE NAMES, in one order, and the THIRD MAN'S TALLY — 23, and 23 is the one distinctive number in the return, the other four being 26/26/20/20 or 20/20/20/20. It is that 23 that carries the identification, and it carries it BECAUSE the printings disagree elsewhere: two independent renderings of one document, differing where OCR and transcription differ, landing on the same odd number against the same seat. A vote count is not a name and cannot be resembled. (2) THE FOLDED CARD IS MINTED FROM THAT BOARD DOING ITS BUSINESS. `beaubien_medore_b`'s whole 1835 evidence is one press reading, chicago_democrat_1833_12_10#c006, and c006 is an ORDINANCE: 'Be it further Ordained by the Board of Trustees of the town of Chicago, That G. W. Dole, Medore B. Beaubien, Edmund S. Kimber[l]y and John Miller, be appointed a Committee to make a contract' — issue page 3, column 5, lines 2695-2701. Those four are four of the five names on the return, the fifth being Owen the president; the board is appointing its own members. So the Medore B. Beaubien of the Democrat is sitting in the seat the Madore card documents, and the town has ALREADY ruled the same column's other spelling question the same way: Edmund S. Kimberly, named in this very ordinance, was folded from three cards onto one in T-0839 and from a fourth in T-1001. (3) THE MIDDLE NAME IS PRINTED WHOLE ON BOTH SIDES. T-0961's landed merge in data/research/books/crosswalk.json carries the reasoning and this ruling does not repeat it: Moses and Kirkland's settlers table prints 'Beaubien, Medore Benj' with nativity Chicago and an empty year cell — the only blank year in a column running 1804 to 1829 that is not a ditto, which is what a native's row looks like — and the survivor's card is Madore BENJAMIN Beaubien, son of Jean Baptiste by Mah-naw-bun-no-quah, born at the settlement. That merge's own rule says it plainly: 'Medore and Madore are the same name spelled two ways by every source that prints it.' (4) ONE BEARER. The town's Beaubien cards are Jean Baptiste and his household, Mark and his, John S., Charles H., Alexandre, B., Medard, and these two. None of the others is a B. Beaubien of the trustee board, and no source reached prints a second Madore or Medore Beaubien at this town — not Andreas, not either Moses and Kirkland volume, not the press corpus, not the tax list of 1833 or the polls of 1833, 1834 and 1835, not the land register, whose Beaubien purchasers are Mark and J. B. WHAT THE MERGE GAINS: the folded card stands `unplaced` with `present_on_scene_date: uncertain` and no dwelling; the survivor is in the south division, in the log house and store at the south-west corner of South Water and Dearborn, present on the scene date, with the trade, the 1831 county licence and the kin row to his father. rulings.for_merge: One letter of the surname and an identical forename, and the shape a transcriber's slip usually takes: davis_john is anchored — John Davis of the Steamboat Hotel, advertising in the American in the scene year itself, his tenure running to 9 November 1835 when Dorsey and Force took the management — while david_john is a projected resident on a single appearance, no trade, no address, no second source. A one-letter surname standing beside an anchor is exactly the pair C9 was written to weigh.
rulings.against_merge: THE ROLL ENTERS BOTH, ONE LINE APART, AND IT IS THE SAME ROLL BOTH CARDS CITE. The tax list of the Town of Chicago for 1833 — a closed roll of 115 enumerated taxpayers, alphabetical — prints “David, John” as its entry 23 (tax_1833_023, transcription line 75) and “Davis, John” as its entry 24 (tax_1833_024, line 76), consecutive, between 'Cook, Thomas' and 'Dole, George W.'. A tax roll enters each taxpayer once; two adjacent lines is the document's own count of how many men of that name it held, and it is not the printer's hand wavering, because a wavering hand does not produce two lines where it meant one — it produces one line spelled the other way, which is what the Pearson cluster above is made of. The rolls go on keeping them apart: the poll filed 11 August 1834 enters “Davis, John” (poll_1834_032, line 201) and no David at all, and the whole IRAD run holds no third bearer of either stem. Nothing else reached is caught setting the two spellings for one man; the one page that sets them both sets them as two. D5, and the cards stay two. `for_merge` is kept verbatim so the argument survives its refusal.
rulings.note: The town holds a second David-stem card, david_harris ('Harris David'), which the voter crosswalk counted when it read this entry — so 'David' is a surname this corpus carries in its own right and not only as a slip for Davis. Note also what davis_john's own card already declines to resolve: a 'Mr. Davis' took over the Sauganash Hotel in 1835 and whether that is this man is unknown. That question is untouched here.

rulings.for: THE PAGE C9 ASKS FOR, AND THE REGISTER SETS BOTH SPELLINGS IN ONE WEEK. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register — one register, one land office, one sale — enters this purchaser under BOTH spellings within two days of each other in June 1835: “PEARSONS H” on 26 June 1835 (ls entries 0001277 E2NE sec 10 T39N R13E, 0001278 E2NE sec 26 T39N R13E, 0002392 E2NW sec 10, 0002393 E2NW sec 24, and the rest of the 26 federal entries the card already carries) and “PEARSON H” on 25 and 26 June 1835 (0016433 SE sec 08 T38N R13E, 0026652 W2NE sec 32 T38N R12E, 0027773 W2NW sec 24 T38N R12E, 0029972 W2SW sec 28 T38N R12E). It does it again with the forename in full at the town lots of 28 June 1836 — “PEARSON HIRAM” (0382941 L7BL1CHI, 0382942 L10BL1CHIV, 0382943 L9BL1CHIV, 0382944 L8BL1CHIV) beside the “PEARSONS HIRAM” rows elsewhere in the same register. Counted over the deposited tables the register sets the stem 127 times with the S and 12 times without it. AND A REGISTER OF TRANSACTIONS IS NOT A ROLL OF PERSONS: it enters one buyer once per parcel and this buyer 47 times, so two spellings inside one week are the clerk's hand and not two men — the distinction D5 turns on, firing the other way one cluster below. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS SET BOTH TOO, AND NEVER ON ONE ROLL. The IRAD lists print “Pearson, Hiram” on the poll of the first election of the Board of Trustees, 10 August 1833 (poll_1833_022, line 43) and on the tax list of 1833 (tax_1833_082, line 134), and “Pearsons, Hiram” on the poll filed 11 August 1834 (poll_1834_087, line 256). Each of those rolls enters a man once; not one of them enters both spellings; the spelling changes BETWEEN rolls and a year apart. That is a printer varying, and it is the opposite of what the 1833 tax roll does to David and Davis. THIS PROJECT'S OWN CARD ALREADY HOLDS THE TWO SPELLINGS AS ONE MAN. hh_pearsons_hiram is built on Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 — 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' — and the line Andreas prints there reads “Hiram Pearson, came in spring of 1833”, without the S. The survivor's arrival, its grade and its trade all rest on a page that spells him the folded card's way. ONE BEARER, AND NOTHING PLACES TWO. The whole resident layer holds exactly two cards on the stem and both are Hiram; the voter crosswalk considered one bearer of 'Pearson' and one of 'Pearsons' and found no rival for either; no source reached puts two Hiram Pearsons at this town at once.
rulings.against: The register's own residence column reads UNKNOWN on every one of these rows, so a purchase places nobody and the register is evidence about a NAME and not about a residence — which is all this ruling asks of it. The one real argument for two men is geographic: the four “PEARSON H” quarter-sections lie in T38N R12E and T38N R13E while “PEARSONS H” buys in T39N R13E, and a reader could hold that those are two speculators who share an initial. Against that stand the same week, the same office and the same sale; the forename printed IN FULL on both sides of the variation in 1836; the town's rolls carrying one Hiram of the stem and not two; and Andreas printing the survivor's own man without the S. Were a second Hiram Pearson of any spelling ever read at this town in this window, this is the ruling to reopen. Nothing here widens compatible(): T-1001 measured a blanket one-letter fold and it is still refused; this is one cluster, ruled at the page. AND THE ONE PAGE A READER WOULD RAISE AGAINST THIS DOES NOT FIRE. Until this ruling, crosswalk_fergus_1843.py refused the pair in D5's own words — 'a directory does not enter one person twice under two spellings' — because Fergus 1843 prints two entries under Pearson and one under Pearsons. Read the three and the argument dissolves: the volume's Pearsons are “Pearson, George Tiffany” and “Pearson, Parker H., clerk”, and the only Hiram in the alphabet is “Pearsons, Hiram, speculator, bds Tremont House” (f1843_e1971, fergus_26_29.txt line 4042). The volume never sets this man's name two ways; it sets it once, with the S, and the two Pearsons beside him are two other men. A directory eight years after the scene date entering a surname twice is not the same instrument as one closed roll entering one FORENAME AND SURNAME twice, which is what the 1833 tax list does to David and Davis and what nothing does here.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is pearsons_hiram because it is the card that carries everything a merge onto the other would lose: the trade (speculator, off Andreas), the arrival ('came in spring of 1833', attested, season precision), the division (south), present_on_scene_date `present` on the city treasurership of 1837-9 and the aldermanry of 1837, and the register's 47 entries. pearson_hiram is a civic mint — occupation none_recorded, division unplaced, present_on_scene_date uncertain — and mint_civic_residents.py writes those three onto every card it derives, so a merge the other way would be re-derived away at the next mint. THE FOLD IS NOT FREE TO THE SURVIVOR, IT GAINS BY IT: the 1833 poll and the 1833 tax entries are on the folded card alone, and the survivor's own civic block cited only the poll of 1834. The folded card carries no fact the survivor's record contradicts — `uncertain` is an absence of reach, not a denial of presence.
rulings.note: T-1130 found this pair from the other side of the room: T-0987 stretch 15 was reading Fergus 1843's initial-absent refusals and could not join “Pearsons, Hiram, speculator, bds Tremont House” to a town card spelled Pearson. The volume was never at fault. The town was, and it is one card less from here.

rulings.for: THE COUNT T-1132 ASKED FOR, RUN OVER THE WHOLE ROLL AND PRINTED. T-1132 left this pair undecided under U1 and wrote down exactly what would settle it — 'Not a page but a COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname' — and refused to take either reading until the count existed. It now does, at tools/exhaust_tax_1833.py, in three gates the build re-derives. (1) THE ROLL HAS TO CARRY HIM, AND THE GROUND IS INSIDE THE LINE. The 1833 tax list is a roll of the OWNERS AND ESTATES of ground inside the town — this project's own finding (T-1117, town_findings_voter_lists v005, which settled it out of the list's own membership: its entry 110 is Alexander Wolcott, three years dead, and what was taxed was the ground he left). The Illinois State Archives tract register enters PRUYNE P for lot 3 of block 119 of the school section on 25 October 1833, a row T-0850 upheld to this survivor on the PEARSONS H argument — the same register writes the purchaser out in full on four other rows and the town holds no second Pruyne for the initial to belong to. Block 119's polygon, measured off J. S. Wright's 1834 survey (T-0797), falls with ALL FOUR corners inside the ring the Trustees walked in their first village ordinance of 7 November 1833 (chicago_democrat_1833_11_26#c024, tier 1, resolved by tools/measure_corporation_limits.py): north of Jackson, east of Jefferson, west of State. So Peter Pruyne owned ground inside the corporate limits of the Town of Chicago in 1833, and that is not a claim about his name. (2) THE TEST DISCRIMINATES, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH ANYTHING. His other 1833 ground does NOT count and the measurement prints it: lots 1 and 8 of block 23, bought 24 October 1833 under the register's fullest spelling PRUYNE PETER, fall with all four corners OUTSIDE the line, west of Jefferson. A gate that said yes to every parcel would be saying nothing. (3) THE EXHAUSTION. All 115 entries of the roll are scored by the letters between the surname each prints and 'pruyne'. The histogram is 1:1, 3:1, 4:4, 5:37, 6:37, 7:18, 8:11, 9:4, 10:2. ONE entry stands within one letter, and it is number 86, 'Pryne, Peter' (line 138) — the single deletion of a u. The next nearest entry on the whole roll is number 85, 'Price, Jeremiah', THREE letters away and carrying a forename that is not Peter and a card of its own that this survivor is not. Nothing stands in the gap. The count is run over the surname and not the forename deliberately: thirteen of the 115 entries print no forename at all — Blinn, Bourison, Church, Jameson, Kingsbury, Magill, Nale, Norton, Post, Sherman, Washburn, Weaver, Whistler — so a count over the bearers of 'Peter' could never close, and each of those thirteen is excluded on its surname instead, at five letters or more. 'Pryne, Peter' is the only entry on this roll that Peter Pruyne can be. (4) NO CLERK IS CAUGHT DISTINGUISHING THEM. D5 refuses where one closed roll enters both spellings side by side; the measurement scores every committed source TEXT in the corpus for the stem and no source prints both. The twenty texts that carry it split cleanly: the IRAD voter and tax rolls and Genealogy Trails' republication of them print Pryne and never Pruyne; Fergus, Moses & Kirkland, the old-settler death notices, the Chicago American and the whole deposited Democrat run print Pruyne and never Pryne. The two bodies never touch, which is what left C9 with no page — and it is also why no roll is on record entering the man twice. (5) ONE BEARER, AND THE FOLDED CARD CONTRADICTS NOTHING. The corpus holds exactly two cards of the stem and no third, folded cards included, and the gate asserts that. `pryne_peter` is a bare civic mint: a name, three appearances on the town's own rolls (tax_1833_086, poll_1834_091, poll_1835_060), no trade, no dwelling, no origin, no family, no party. There is nothing on it for the survivor's record to contradict, and everything on it — the 1833 roll, the 1834 poll and the 1835 poll — is what a Chicago druggist who bought town ground in October 1833, married in August 1835 and polled in ward 1 in May 1837 was missing from his record.
rulings.against: WHAT IS STILL NOT THERE, AND IT IS THE THING C9 ASKS FOR. No publication is caught setting both spellings for one man, and this ruling does not pretend one is: the 239 printings of the stem in the 1833-1835 Democrat are all Pruyne, the IRAD rolls are all Pryne, and Genealogy Trails carrying both is a republisher's inconsistency across two different originals, which is not a printer's inside one. C9 CANNOT FIRE HERE AND IS NOT INVOKED. THE REFUSAL THIS OVERTURNS, NAMED RATHER THAN STEPPED AROUND. D7 — written the night before this ruling, by T-1134 — is the standing refusal for precisely this shape, and it describes this pair in its own text: two spellings standing on instruments that never touch, 'a tax roll against a newspaper'. Every one of D7's three conditions holds here. It is not applied because D7's own reasoning says what would displace it — 'nothing reached folds them', and 'a later page reopens it' — and something reached does. It is not a page: it is a count, which is admissible where a page is not because it never weighs how alike the two strings look.
