C14 states that relationship in its own text and says to reach for D7 first. THE RESIDUAL, WRITTEN OUT RATHER THAN SMOOTHED AWAY. The roll prints no day within 1833, so nothing dates the assessment, and if it was taken before 22 October 1833 the ground argument reaches nothing. That end is bounded and not closed: the Town of Chicago did not exist before 10 August 1833, and this corpus holds no statement of its bounds earlier than the ordinance of 7 November 1833 — thirteen days AFTER the purchase that carries this ruling. So the roll is a roll of the town's last months of 1833 at the earliest and he stood inside its line for all of them. That is an INFERENCE about the assessment's date, it is graded as one in the measurement's `what_it_does_not_say`, and a dated 1833 assessment turning up before 22 October reopens this ruling. THE ARGUMENT THIS RULING DOES NOT USE. 'He bought at the town's own school-section sale, so he is the kind of man the tax roll carries' is T-1017's question, and T-1017 measured it and REFUSED it: at that sale thirteen of 105 buyers carry a surname the layer holds nobody of, only 50 of 105 carry an upheld match, and the sale prints twenty surnames more than one way with PRUYNE — P, P AND CO, PETER — expressly among them. None of that is relied on here. What is relied on is narrower and is geometry: where two named parcels of his lie against a line the gate re-derives, with two more of his lying outside it. WHAT THE MERGE COSTS. The town's person count falls by one, from two men of one stem to one. `pryne_peter` is graded attested on the 1835 poll with a second list behind it, so this is not a weak card being swept into a strong one — it is the reason T-1132 said the pair was worth deciding. Its whole record is carried: the three roll appearances arrive on the survivor through the card-merge crosswalk, and the card itself is kept entire under data/residents/merged/. NOTHING IS PROMOTED TO MAKE THIS TIDY. No grade moves by this ruling, no dwelling is assigned, and `present_on_scene_date` is not touched: T-1117 already refused tax_1833 as a leg of the presence bracket and that refusal stands, so the survivor is no more placed in the town on 1 July 1835 after this merge than before it.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is `pruyne_peter`, the card that carries the trade — Peter Pruyne the druggist, who with Edmund Stoughton Kimberly opened Chicago's second drug store early in 1833 — and he is a PARTNER in hh_pruyne_kimberly rather than its head, the same shape as the two Kimberly rows, so the merge lands on the person and the household's other partner is untouched. What the folded card brings that the survivor did not have: the town's own 1833 tax roll, the 1834 poll list and the 1835 poll list, under the spelling those rolls print. What it does not bring is a residence — see `against`.
rulings.for_merge: Peter Pruyne is one of the better-documented men in the town — with Edmund Stoughton Kimberly he opened Chicago's second drug store early in 1833; he bought lot 1 of block 23 and lot 3 of block 119 of the school section on 24 and 25 October 1833 and town lots after; he married Rebecca Sherman on 20 August 1835; he polled in ward 1 at the first city election of 2 May 1837; Genealogy Trails' early-settler death notices print 'Pruyne, Peter, died November, 1839'. A man of that standing is one the town's own tax and poll rolls should carry, and the only entry of the stem on any of them is “Pryne, Peter” — tax_1833_086 (line 138), poll_1834_091 (line 260) and poll_1835_060 (line 347). The resident layer holds exactly one card of each spelling and no other bearer of the stem at all.
rulings.against_merge: THE PAGE C9 ASKS FOR DOES NOT EXIST, and C9's demonstration is its load-bearing clause. No publication reached is caught setting both spellings. The IRAD rolls print Pryne three times and Pruyne never. The ISA land register prints 'PRUYNE P', 'PRUYNE P AND CO' and 'PRUYNE PETER' eighteen times and Pryne never. The whole deposited 1833-1835 newspaper run prints the stem 239 times, every one of them Pruyne. Moses & Kirkland print Pruyne and Pruyn; Fergus prints Pruyne. The two bodies of evidence never touch: the town's rolls know only Pryne, and the books, the press and the register know only Pruyne. Folding on what is left — one letter — is precisely what T-1001 measured and refused. AND THE TWO SPELLINGS APPEAR ON ONE SITE WITHOUT MEETING ON ONE PAGE: Genealogy Trails carries 'Pruyne, Peter' in earlysettlerobits and 'Pryne, Peter' in polllist, but those are its transcriptions of two different ORIGINALS, and a republisher's inconsistency across two documents is not a printer's inconsistency inside one, which is the thing C9 asks for.

clusters.why_not_derived: THE CANDIDATE TEST BUCKETS BY SURNAME AND FOLDS THE SURNAME EXACTLY. `clusters()` in tools/consolidate_town_cards.py groups the town's cards by the surname as printed, so `pruyne` and `pryne` are two buckets and the two cards never meet, however exactly their forenames agree. Widening that fold is NOT done here, and T-1001 measured why — see C9 and tools/measure_surname_fold.py. The cluster is written into this file by hand, as the Kimberley row is, so the ruling is read by the same machinery as every other.

rulings.for: ONE PRINTED LINE, READ TWO WAYS, AND THIS PROJECT MINTED A CARD FROM EACH READING. It is not two printings of one man's name. It is one line. Both cards' own arrival blocks already say, in the same words, that they stand on the SAME return — the Chicago post office's list of letters remaining on 1 January 1834 — which the Democrat reprinted over nine impressions. hh_fraser_wm_h is minted from the impression of 28 January 1834, column 1, which sets “Wm. H. Fraser”. hh_frazer_wm_h is minted from the impression of 4 March 1834, column 26, whose line is damaged and reads “il. Frazer”, normalized “Wm. H. Frazer”. T-0424 read the NINTH impression at the page image and set the return down in printed order — 170 lines, data/research/newspapers/letter_list_1834_01_01_printed.json — and T-1010's concordance then tied every extracted name to its line. LINE 55 CARRIES BOTH: `tied_by: image` to chicago_democrat_1834_03_04#c026 (“il. Frazer”) and `tied_by: spelling` to chicago_democrat_1834_01_28#c001 (“Wm. H. Fraser”), and the row already records `also_resolved_to: [person_wm_h_frazer]` beside the person it reaches. So the demonstration C9 asks for stands at its maximum: not a printer varying between two lines, but ONE line of one roll that two impressions of one paper read differently — tied together at the scan, and committed in this tree since T-1010, while the two cards went on standing apart. The forename and middle initial agree on both readings and on the image; the whole corpus holds exactly one bearer of “Wm. H.” on the stem and the gazetteer carries no other; the resident layer holds one card of each spelling and nothing else; and the folded card carries no fact the survivor contradicts — both are letter-list-only, no trade, no street, no household, present_on_scene_date `uncertain`.
rulings.against: THE STEM IS NOT UNIQUE AT THIS TOWN, and that is said here rather than left out. The raw OCR of the Democrat of 29 July 1835 carries “Jobo Frazer” — almost certainly John Frazer — in a later return this project has never extracted, so a Frazer who is not this man was at the office eighteen months on. C9 asks for one bearer of the FORENAME AND MIDDLE INITIAL, not one bearer of the stem, and “Wm. H.” has one; were a second Wm. H. of either spelling ever read at this town in this window, this is the ruling to reopen. THE SECOND ARGUMENT IS ABOUT THE SURVIVOR'S NAME AND NOT ABOUT THE FOLD: the image is a witness of higher rank than either transcription and it sets FRAZER, so the surviving card wears the weaker reading's spelling. That is a real defect, and it is deliberately NOT repaired here — it is a question about what the line says, not about how many men it names, T-1010's concordance already records it as one of nineteen `name_differs` rows, and T-1139 owns the class. Nothing here widens compatible(): this is one cluster, ruled at the page, and T-1001's refusal of a blanket one-letter fold stands.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the card the concordance's own tie already points at — line 55 `reaches` person_wm_h_fraser / hh_fraser_wm_h, with person_wm_h_frazer named as the reading it also resolved to — so the merge lands where this project's committed reading of the page already put the line and nothing downstream has to be re-pointed. What the folded card brings is the impression of 4 March 1834, which is the reading the page image agrees with; the survivor held only the 28 January one.
rulings.note: Found by putting `surname_one_letter_away.town_pairs` over the letter-list cohort and then asking, for each pair, WHICH RETURN each card stands on — a question the mint answers on every card it writes and which no merge pass had ever read. Five of T-1133's seven pairs stand on two different returns and are refused under D6; this pair and Vandine/Vandino stand on one, and one is enough.

rulings.for: THE SAME SHAPE AS FRASER/FRAZER, ON THE SAME RETURN, AND IT IS THE SAME TWO IMPRESSIONS THAT DISAGREE. Both cards' arrival blocks stand on the Chicago post office's return of 1 January 1834. hh_vandino_john is minted from the impression of 28 January 1834, column 1, which sets “John Vandino”; hh_vandine_john from the impression of 4 March 1834, column 27, whose line prints the surname alone — as_printed “Vandine”, normalized “John Vandine”. T-1010's concordance of the return ties BOTH to LINE 158 of T-0424's reading of the ninth impression at the page image: `tied_by: image` to chicago_democrat_1834_03_04#c027 and `tied_by: spelling` to chicago_democrat_1834_01_28#c001, with `also_resolved_to: [person_john_vandine]` on the row. One line, two readings, two cards. The forename agrees wherever it is printed — the 28 January impression and the image both set “John”, and the 4 March impression prints no forename at all, so nothing contradicts; the gazetteer holds no other bearer of the stem, and the nearest names on the 28 January line-run are different stems entirely (Adam Vandorwerk, Vanderwerker, Vanzandt); and the folded card carries no fact the survivor contradicts, both being letter-list-only with no trade, no street and present_on_scene_date `uncertain`.
rulings.against: The 4 March impression prints no forename, so strictly what it sets is a SURNAME, and a surname with no forename is what R1 refuses to attach to anybody. R1 does not reach this cluster, and the reason is the line number rather than the letters: the forename on that card is not an inference from the other card, it is T-0424's reading of the same line at the page image, which sets “John Vandine” in full. Take the image away and this is R1 and the cards stay two. AND THE SURVIVOR'S SPELLING IS THE WEAKER ONE HERE TOO: the image reads VANDINE where the surviving card reads Vandino. As at line 55, that is T-1139's question and not this one's — the fold is about how many men line 158 names, and the answer does not depend on which of two readings of it the card wears.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is again the card the concordance's tie names — line 158 `reaches` person_john_vandino / hh_vandino_john — so the landed merge agrees with the committed reading and the redirect table carries vandine_john onto it. The folded card brings the 4 March 1834 impression, the one the image agrees with.
rulings.note: That BOTH of T-1133's merges are the same two impressions of one return is the pass's second finding and is worth keeping: the Democrat's compositor reset this return between 28 January and 4 March 1834, and the two settings differ in at least two names out of 170. T-1010's `name_differs` list counts nineteen rows of that kind over the whole return, of which these two had been minted twice; the rest reach one card each and are T-1139's.

rulings.for_merge: One letter at the end of a French-Canadian surname, an identical forename, one office, one paper and one kind of list. Babeu and Babeue are the same word with and without its terminal e, the Chicago post office held a letter for each inside six months, and the town's whole knowledge of both is those two lines. On resemblance alone this is the most merge-like pair of the seven.
rulings.against_merge: TWO RETURNS, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. “Joseph Babeu” is LINE 10 of the return of 1 January 1834, read at the page image by T-0424 and tied there by T-1010's concordance to the one impression that carries it, the Democrat of 4 March 1834, column 33 — a single tie, no second reading, no disagreement on the row. “Joseph Babeue” stands on the return of 1 July 1834, printed in the impressions of 9 July (“oseph Babeue”, the initial lost) and 16 July 1834 (“Joseph Babeue”) — two impressions of that later return, agreeing with each other and both against the January spelling. So the office closed two returns six months apart, entered one spelling on each, and was never asked to set them together: C9's demonstration is absent and D5's is absent with it. Neither card is an anchor — no trade, no dwelling, no research on either — and neither name appears anywhere else in the corpus; the gazetteer holds these two and no other bearer of the stem. What is left to fold on is one letter, which is what T-1001 measured and refused. D6, and the cards stay two.
rulings.note: The two returns are the pair's whole discriminator and it cuts both ways: six months is long enough for a second Joseph of a French-Canadian name to reach a town that was taking in hundreds, and short enough for one man to have two letters waiting. Nothing decides it, which is what D6 says. A tenth impression of either return, or any source outside the post office naming either man, reopens this at once.

rulings.for_merge: An interior letter, e against n, in a five-letter surname, with “Reuben” identical on both. e and n are neighbours in worn type and in OCR alike, and the town holds nothing of either man but a name on a post office list — the classic shape of one record minted twice.
rulings.against_merge: TWO RETURNS NINE MONTHS APART, EACH INTERNALLY CONSISTENT. “Reuben Beech” stands on the return of 1 July 1834 and is printed TWICE, in the impressions of 9 July 1834 (“leaben Beech”, the forename wrecked, the surname clean) and 16 July 1834 (“Reuben Beech”): two settings of that return, and both set BEECH. “Bench, Reuben” stands on the return of 31 March 1835, printed in the Democrat of 20 May 1835, clean and alphabetically seated between “Beaubien” and “Bennet” in the B run. Two impressions on one side and a clean line on the other means the one-letter difference is NOT a damaged impression that a better one repairs — the readings are stable within each return and differ only between them. No return sets both, neither card is an anchor, and the gazetteer holds no third bearer of either stem. D6.
rulings.note: The alphabetical seat is worth recording and is not decisive: BENCH is correctly placed in the 20 May 1835 B run, so the compositor set the letters he meant to set, and BEECH is correctly placed in its own. Two correctly-alphabetised entries nine months apart are exactly what two men look like and exactly what one man written to twice by two correspondents looks like. Note also that the return of 31 March 1835 supplies the second spelling of THREE of T-1133's pairs — Bench, Murry and Squire — against the return of 1 July 1834's Beech and Murray; a reader tempted to treat that as a house style should weigh that the same 1835 return also sets Hussey against the 1834 return's Hussy, which is the opposite direction.

rulings.for_merge: One letter, “Robert” on both, and the two returns bracket the scene date: “Hussy, Robert 2” on the return of 1 October 1834 and “Hussey, Robert” on the return of 1 July 1835, the scene date itself. A man with two letters waiting in the autumn of 1834 and another the following summer is a plausible single correspondent, and the surname is one whose two spellings were both current.
rulings.against_merge: TWO RETURNS, NINE MONTHS APART, NEITHER SETTING BOTH. “Hussy, Robert 2” is printed in the Democrat of 22 October 1834, seated between “Williams, Charles C.” and “Winters, Moses” in a surname-first list; “Hussey, Robert” in the Democrat of 1 July 1835, between “Phillips James” and “Park Hezekiah”. Each reading is clean in its own impression and neither return carries the other spelling. Neither card is an anchor; the gazetteer holds these two and no third bearer; nothing outside the post office names either man. C9's page does not exist and D5's roll does not either. D6.
rulings.note: This pair carries the strongest single argument FOR a merge in the seven and it still does not reach: the 1835 return is the one dated 1 July 1835, the scene date, so a fold would move a man from `uncertain` to the day the reconstruction stands on. That is a reason to want the merge and not a reason to make it, and the ruling is written down here so the next pass does not mistake the appetite for the evidence.

rulings.for_merge: Murray and Murry differ by one letter and both cards read “Alonzo”, which is an uncommon forename — the town holds one other Alonzo in the whole resident layer. Two uncommon forenames on one stem inside a year is the shape a duplicate usually takes.
rulings.against_merge: THREE THINGS, AND THE FIRST TWO WOULD BE ENOUGH. (1) TWO RETURNS, AND THE EARLIER IS SET THREE TIMES. “Alonzo Murray” stands on the return of 1 July 1834 and is printed in the impressions of 2, 9 and 16 July 1834, all three reading “Alonzo Murray”; “Murry, Alanzo 2” stands on the return of 31 March 1835, printed 20 May 1835. No return sets both. (2) THE FORENAMES ARE NOT IDENTICAL AS PRINTED. The 1835 line reads ALANZO, not Alonzo; the cards agree only after this project's own normalizer folded the o/a. So the pair that town_pairs joined on an identical forename does not have one on the page, and a merge would be folding two letters, not one. (3) MURRAY IS A POPULATED SURNAME AT THIS TOWN WHERE MURRY IS NOT. The corpus carries Nelson Murray (return of 1 April 1834), “A, MURRAY” in the Democrat of 24 September 1834 and James H. Murray in the American of 20 June 1835, and the resident layer carries a Patrick Murray card besides; the only Murry of any forename is this one. A surname several families bear is not a slip for a surname one man bears, and the direction of the supposed error is therefore unargued. D6, and the cards stay two.
rulings.note: Pass 02 of the resident-research programme reached this pair from the other side and recorded the same answer — “strong duplicate candidates from one-letter variants in consecutive-year Chicago returns; no independent identity record resolves them”, and “remain separate until a record or scan links the spellings”. Pass 13 adds that St Cyr's 1837 “S. Murry” is refused on the forename and so does not supply the link. This ruling agrees with both and adds the return test and the Alanzo reading, which neither pass had.

settled_from.by: the page images of the 1 April 1834 return, read at T-1138

rulings.for_merge: “Geo.” is the ordinary abbreviation of “George”, Square and Squire differ by one letter, and the resident layer holds one card of each and no other bearer of either stem. Pass 06 of the resident-research programme reached the pair and wrote it down as a possible duplicate: “Geo. Square may be a transcription/duplicate relation to George Squire”.
rulings.against_merge: THE LINE IS READ, AND IT MOVED THE CARD BEFORE IT COULD BE WEIGHED. T-1133 left this pair UNDECIDED under U1 because one of its two printed lines had two readings: the extraction of the Democrat of 1 April 1834 set it “3. Geo. Square t 3 first rate” and the extraction of the 16 April impression set the same position “Geo. Saver”, and a merge cannot be tested against a line nobody has settled. T-1138 read all THREE impressions the paper printed of that one return — 1 April, 8 April and 16 April, at the scan the deposit manifest names — and all three set the same five letters: “Geo. Squar”. `Saver` is not on the page; the second letter is a q with its descender. And `Square` is one letter too long: there is no final e on any impression, and on two of the three the line ends in clean paper where an e would have to stand. So the card the mint carried as `square_geo` is withdrawn and the same person stands as `squar_geo`, under the name the page sets. THAT ALONE WOULD ANSWER THE CLUSTER — Squar and Squire are not one letter apart, so the one-letter test that raised this pair no longer reaches it — but the refusal is not rested on the spelling alone, because the spelling is exactly what was in doubt. D6 is reached on the evidence's shape, which the reading did not change: neither card is an anchor, the town's whole knowledge of both is the post office's returns, `Squar` stands on the return of 1 April 1834 and `Squire` on the return of 31 March 1835, and NO single return sets both spellings — so C9's demonstration is absent and D5's counter-demonstration is absent with it. The roll is serial; it was never asked the question. The cards stay two, and that is NOT a claim that the town held two men of the name.
rulings.note: What the image cost the merge case is worth stating plainly, because it is the whole movement of this ticket: the pair looked mergeable on a one-letter distance that the page does not support. Two letters now separate the printed names, and the only reading that would have DISSOLVED the pair outright — `Saver`, which would have made `square_geo` no Square at all — is the one the page refutes hardest. A source outside the post office naming either man, or a single return that sets both spellings, reopens this at once.

rulings.for: THE LIST'S OWN ALPHABET SAYS THE SURNAME BEGINS WITH K, AND THE READING DOES NOT. hh_anight_clark stands on ONE line of ONE document: the post office's list of letters remaining at Chicago on 30 June 1835, printed in the Chicago Democrat of 1 July 1835, page 3 column 4, where this project's extraction reads it '& Anight, Clark' (chicago_democrat_1835_07_01#c005, quote line 191). That column weaves TWO alphabetical runs of the one list line by line — an F-to-L run and an M-to-S run — and the extraction's own locator says so and lists which lines belong to the list. Read the F-to-L run alone across the lines either side of it and it is the K section throughout: 'K.' (the section letter, line 187), 'Kirne, E. Capt.' (189), '& Anight, Clark' (191), 'King, Neheminh' (193), 'Keys, Ed. or Jos. Keys' (195), 'Kooken, James' (198), 'Kent, Alex. M.' (200), 'King, Elans A.' (202), 'King, Henry Hon.' (204). Every other name in that run is a K. The deviation is at the FIRST letter and the character standing where the K should be is '&' — a broken capital, which is what the rest of that same reading is full of ('Bobinson George IS.' for Robinson, 'Rius Archibald' for Rice, 'Scot' and 'Seston' beside 'Seaton'). 'ANIGHT' IS NOT A NAME THIS CORPUS HOLDS. Searched across every deposited text and every extracted claim, the string occurs exactly twice outside this project's own derived files, and both are this one reading. No directory, no roll, no book, no paper sets it. 'Knight' is set constantly, including by the town's own poll of 1834. AND THE RESTORED LETTER LANDS ON A CARD THE TOWN ALREADY HOLDS, UNDER THE SAME FORENAME. hh_knight_clark is minted off poll_1834 — 'Knight, Clark' (voter_lists_1833_1835.txt line 238) — and 'Clark' as a forename is rare enough that the town holds exactly one bearer of it on this stem. The other Knight the town holds is John, on poll_1835, and he is untouched. THE EXTRACTION PASS ITSELF REFERRED THIS HERE. Its note on the column reads: 'A name whose initial is present but disagrees with its section is a MISREADING, not a clipping, and stands as printed — correcting it would be a guess, and identity.json is the only place two spellings may become one person.' It was right to leave it, and this is the place it left it for.
rulings.against: The two runs do not alternate perfectly — line 197 ('Sherman m. c.') is a second M-to-S line with no F-to-L line between it and 196 — so the weave is not a machine the reading can be decoded by, and the argument rests on the SECTION rather than on the parity of lines. It does not need the parity: every F-to-L name from 189 to 204 is a K, whichever way the extra line is counted. A reader could also hold that a letter list is not a list a section letter binds, since an uncalled-for letter is filed under the clerk's reading of an address and not under the person's own spelling — but that objection argues for the fold and not against it, because it makes the list's letter the best evidence about the surname and the reading the worst. What would genuinely reopen this is a scan read of page 3 column 4 that shows the printed entry really does begin with an A. The extraction offers three separate transcriptions of that column and none does. Nothing here widens compatible(): T-1001's blanket fold is still refused, and this is one cluster, ruled at the column.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is knight_clark because its reading is the one the alphabet vindicates and because it is the card the town's own record made: poll_1834, transcribed by IRAD, against a scan-OCR of a newspaper's uncalled-letter list. The fold is not free to the survivor, it gains by it — hh_knight_clark's arrival bound was 1834-12-31 'not later than' off the poll alone, and the folded card carries a second appearance, the letter of 30 June 1835, which is somebody writing to this name at Chicago a day before the scene date. Nothing on hh_anight_clark contradicts the survivor: both are projected residents with no trade, no dwelling and no division.
rulings.note: Found by T-1130's town_pairs test and ruled under a rule this pair needed written for it. C9 could not reach it because C9 asks for one PUBLICATION setting both spellings, and here only one publication has the name at all — the variation is this repository's, not the town's.

rulings.for: ONE PAPER, TEN WEEKS, ONE OFFICE, BOTH SPELLINGS. The Chicago Democrat prints this man as secretary of a public meeting of the town twice in the scene year and spells him two ways: (1) 20 May 1835, page 1 column 3 — 'GREAT DEMOCRATIC MEETING ... held at the Exchange Coffee House ... on Tuesday Evening, April 13, 1835 ... H. HUGUNIN was called to the Chair, and J. W. E[ldre]d[g]e and J. C. GOODHUE appointed Secretaries', the name as printed 'J. W. E.prepce' and settled by the paper's own signature to the proceedings at line 546, 'J.W. ELDREDGE, Secretary' (chicago_democrat_1835_05_20#c001); and (2) 1 July 1835, column 11 — the meeting of 29 June, 'E. B. Williams [was called to the] chair, and John W. Eldridge [appointed] secretary', with 'J. W. Eldridge' again on the committee of fourteen that meeting appointed (chicago_democrat_1835_07_01#c011). That is C9's demonstration in its strongest form: the SAME title, inside the window, setting both spellings of one man discharging one kind of office, with the forename and the middle initial agreeing on every printing. AND TWO DIRECTORIES DO IT AGAIN, WITH A TRADE AND A STREET. Fergus 1843 prints 'Eldridge, John Woodworth, physician, res Randolph, first door west of City Hotel'; Norris 1844 prints 'Eldredge, John W. physician, res Randolph st. east of Clark st'. One trade, one street, consecutive years, the two spellings — and Fergus supplies the middle NAME, Woodworth, which is what the W. of every other printing stands for. ONE BEARER AND NOTHING PLACES TWO. The town holds exactly one card of each spelling, both 'John W.'; the whole corpus reaches no second John W. of either stem at this town; and no source puts two of them here at once.
rulings.against: The two Democrat readings are of different meetings, so a reader could hold that the town had two men who each took a secretary's chair. Against that: the paper prints no other Eldredge or Eldridge of any forename in the whole 1833-1835 run; a town whose Democratic meeting and whose 29 June meeting were minuted by two different men of the same forename and middle initial, differing by one letter of surname, is a coincidence nothing attests; and the directories then put one physician of the name on Randolph Street in two consecutive years under the two spellings. Fergus 1839 also stands on the surviving card, under Eldridge. Nothing here widens compatible(), and T-1001's blanket fold is still refused.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is eldridge_john_w: it carries three sources to the folded card's two (the Democrat, Fergus 1839 and Fergus 1843 against the Democrat and Norris 1844), and it carries the full middle name — Fergus 1843's 'John Woodworth' — which a merge the other way would lose. Both cards are graded attested on the paper, so the fold costs the survivor no grade. The folded card's Norris 1844 entry and its 20 May 1835 secretaryship come across; neither contradicts anything the survivor's record holds.
rulings.note: The one pair of T-1130's nineteen that BOTH the press and the directories demonstrate. Neither card is an anchor by consolidate_town_cards.anchored() — both are mint cards and the mint writes occupation none_recorded — yet the directories print the trade on both sides. That the anchor test cannot see a trade a directory prints on a mint card is a separate finding and is not acted on here.

rulings.for: ONE PAPER, FOUR PRINTINGS, FOUR SPELLINGS, NO TWO ALIKE — AND TWO OF THEM ARE ONE ITEM PRINTED TWICE. The Chicago Democrat sets this man's surname every one of these ways inside the window: 'Stephen M. Salesbuc' (26 November 1833, column 31, attesting an estray appraisal as J.P. — "before Stephen M. Salesbuc, J. P. Attest—RICH'D I. HAMILTON, Clerk Com. Ct. Cook co., Ill."); 'Stephen M. Salisbury' (3 December 1833, column 7, among the men the appraisal names); 'plen M. Salsburg' (6 August 1834, page 3 column 1, the county's general election returns, For County Commissioners: 'ou ta Hunter / des Kinzie / Scaredi / plen M. Salsburg'); and 'Stephen M. Balsbury' (13 August 1834, page 2 column 5, THE SAME SLATE PRINTED WHOLE a week later: 'For County Commissioners: [E]dward E. Hunter, / Isaac Scarret / James Kinzie / Stephen M. Balsbury'). The last two are the load-bearing pair, because they are not two men in two items — they are ONE ROW OF ONE SLATE, printed twice by one paper eight days apart, and the paper spells it two ways. A printer caught varying inside one item is precisely what C9 asks for and precisely what the Pearson cluster folded on. THE OFFICES TIE THE PRINTINGS TO ONE MAN AND THEY ARE THE SAME COUNTY'S. A justice of the peace of Cook County in November 1833 standing for county commissioner of Cook County in August 1834 is one public career, not two; and the surviving card already carries the trade the paper gives, justice_of_the_peace, which the folded card does not. ONE BEARER. The town holds exactly one Stephen M. of each spelling and no other bearer of either stem at all; no source reached puts two Stephen M. Sal-sburys at this town at once.
rulings.against: EVERY ONE OF THE FOUR READINGS IS GARBLED, so strictly the paper is not caught setting 'Salisbury' and 'Salsbury' — it is caught setting Salesbuc, Salisbury, Salsburg and Balsbury, and two of the four spellings in dispute are this repository's own normalisations of those garbles rather than anything a compositor set. That cuts both ways and it is why the fold is right: if no printing sets either spelling cleanly, then nothing stands between the cards except which garble a mint pass rounded which way, and the town has been holding a man twice on the strength of it. The real argument for two men is that the 1833 items and the 1834 slate are joined by the name and the county alone — no vote tally, no signature, no address ties the J.P. to the candidate — so C11's office clause is NOT what fires here and is not claimed. Were a second Stephen M. of this stem ever read at Chicago, this is the ruling to reopen. Nothing here widens compatible().
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is salisbury_stephen_m. It is the `documented` card, not a civic mint: it carries the trade — justice of the peace, attested to the paper — where salsbury_stephen_m carries occupation none_recorded, and mint_civic_residents.py writes none_recorded onto every card it derives, so a merge the other way would be re-derived away at the next mint, which is the same reason the Pearson fold ran the direction it did. It is also the spelling Fergus 1843, Norris 1844, Moses & Kirkland and the Calumet Club registry use for the stem. The folded card brings the candidacy for County Commissioner of August 1834 — a fact the survivor's record did not hold and does not contradict.
rulings.note: The 6 August 1834 column is the county's first general election under the new town, and the extraction's own note on it says the column 'is cut down its left edge by the leading article, so nearly every name survives without its forename' and that every forename there is supplied from the 13 August printing. That supply is what makes the two printings comparable, and it is bracketed as a supply in the record.

rulings.for: ONE PAPER, THREE PRINTINGS OF ONE ISAAC, THREE SPELLINGS. The Chicago Democrat sets this surname: 'Teanc Scarritt' in the post office's list of letters uncalled-for of 28 January 1834, column 1, read as Isaac Scarritt; 'Scaredi' in the county election returns of 6 August 1834, page 3 column 1, read as Isaac Scarrett, For County Commissioners, in the row beside James Kinzie; and 'Isaac Scarret' in the SAME SLATE printed whole on 13 August 1834, page 2 column 5. One title, one man, one forename, inside the window, and not two of the three spellings alike — which is C9's demonstration, and it is doubled here because the August slate is one item the paper set twice and spelled differently each time. AN INDEPENDENT BOOK PUTS AN ISAAC OF THIS STEM AT CHICAGO. Moses & Kirkland's History of Chicago volume 2 prints 'Rev. Isaac Scarritt succeeded Rev. Mr. —' and indexes him 'Scarritt, (Rev.) Isaac, 365'. The same volume's index also holds 'Scarrett, H. M.', a different forename, which is the whole of what the corpus offers against a single bearer — and it is a different man. ONE BEARER OF THE FORENAME. The town holds exactly one Isaac of each spelling and no other bearer of either stem; nothing reached places two Isaacs of it here at once.
rulings.against: The 6 August reading is marked UNCERTAIN by the extraction — 'Scaredi' is a bad enough garble that three separate transcriptions of the column were needed to settle it — so the strongest printing on the Scarrett side is really the 13 August one, 'Isaac Scarret', which is a THIRD spelling and not the card's. That the card's own spelling is set by no printing cleanly is an argument about orthography and not about identity, and it is answered below. The real argument for two men is that one card stands on an uncalled letter and the other on a county candidacy, and nothing but the name joins them; against it stands the paper printing no other Scarr-stem forename in the whole 1833-1835 run, and 'Isaac' being the forename on both.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is scarrett_isaac: graded attested on a contemporary paper naming the man in the town, against scarritt_isaac's `inferred` — a projected resident known from ONE post-office return and nothing else. The candidacy for County Commissioner is the fact that would be lost by a merge the other way. THE SURVIVOR'S SPELLING IS THE PAPER'S SLATE AND MAY NOT BE THE MAN'S: Moses & Kirkland print him Scarritt, and if a later reading of that page carries the identification, the surviving card should be RENAMED rather than re-split — the identity ruled here does not depend on which of the two the display name carries.
rulings.note: Isaac Scarrett and Stephen M. Salsbury stand in the same row of the same slate on the same two pages, and this project had minted both of them twice. Two of T-1130's nineteen, found and ruled together, on one item of one newspaper printed twice.

rulings.for_merge: THREE INITIALS AGREEING IN ORDER IS AS DISTINCTIVE AS A FORENAME GETS. 'A. O. T.' is not J. or W. H.; the corpus holds no second bearer of those three initials under any surname. A. O. T. Breed is a documented man of the county: the Democrat prints a writ 'dated the 20th day of [March, A.] D. 1834, at the suit of A. O. T. Bre[ed, of the said] county of Cook, and State of Illinois' against an estate in the Territory of Michigan for $1,014; it prints 'Cook Circuit Court, May Term, 1834. Bristol, Howard & Wadham[s] vs. A. O. T. Breed'; the letter list of 1 January 1834 carries him; the Second Presbyterian roll carries the surname. A man suing and sued in the county's own court in 1834 is a man who could be expected on the town's poll of 1835, and the only entry on that poll that could be him is 'Bread, A.O.T.'
rulings.against_merge: NO TITLE REACHED SETS BOTH SPELLINGS, AND ONE OF THEM IS SET EXACTLY ONCE IN THE WHOLE CORPUS. Searched word-boundary over every deposited text and every extracted claim: 'Bread' occurs as a SURNAME in exactly one place — the 1835 poll list, 'Bread, A.O.T.' (voter_lists_1833_1835.txt lines 289 and 294, the transcription printing the page twice) — and every other hit in the corpus is the common noun, including Moses & Kirkland's index entry 'Bread, limitation of, price'. 'Breed' is set by the Democrat, by the Second Presbyterian roll ('Breed, Mrs. Amanda'), by genealogytrails' cemetery history and by Moses & Kirkland — and never beside 'Bread'. The two bodies of evidence do not touch: the town's own roll knows only Bread, and the press, the church and the books know only Breed. Folding on what is left — one letter — is what T-1001 measured and refused. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.
rulings.note: The strongest refusal of the six by the gap between what the evidence suggests and what it demonstrates, and it is recorded that way on purpose. Nothing here says the town held two men: it says the page C9 asks for has not been found.

rulings.for_merge: THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS CARRY ONE WILLIAM OF THE STEM AND SPELL HIM TWO WAYS, A YEAR APART AND NEVER ON ONE ROLL — which is the exact shape the Pearson fold rested part of its weight on. The tax list of the Town of Chicago for 1833 prints 'Forsyth, William' (voter_lists_1833_1835.txt line 84); the poll filed 11 August 1834 prints 'Forsythe, William' (line 210). Each of those rolls enters a man once, neither enters both spellings, and the spelling changes between them. The Chicago Democrat of 29 October 1834 then prints 'William Forsyth' in the town. The town holds exactly one William of each spelling and no other bearer of either stem.
rulings.against_merge: THE ONE DOCUMENT THAT SETS BOTH IS A TRANSCRIPTION OF TWO ORIGINALS, WHICH IS THE THING C9 REFUSES TO COUNT. IRAD's 'Early Chicago Voters' PDF holds the 1833 tax list and the 1834 poll between one pair of covers, so a reader can point at one file and see both spellings — but the Pruyne ruling one cluster's-worth of reasoning above already drew this line, and it draws it the same way here: a republisher's inconsistency across two documents is not a printer's inconsistency inside one. Outside the rolls the corpus only ever sets the short form for this man: the Democrat prints Forsyth eleven times across the 1833-1835 run and Forsythe never, and Fergus 1839 prints Forsyth alone. AND ONE TITLE IS CAUGHT TREATING THE TWO AS TWO SURNAMES: the Second Presbyterian Church roll of 1892 populates both, 'Forsyth, Benjamin H. / Daniel S. / Logan Wallace / Robert / Mrs. Kate / Miss Minnie L.' and 'Forsythe, Mrs. Fannie E. / Geo. A. / Frank W. / Miss Jennie / John / Mrs. John' — thirteen people, not one William among them, and the volume alphabetises them as two names. That is not D5 (no closed roll enters both as separate entries for this forename) but it is the corpus declining to hand over the demonstration. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.
rulings.note: Of the six refusals this is the one a scan read could overturn fastest: the IRAD originals are two clerks' hands and the transcription is one typist's, so a reading of the 1834 poll's own page may find the terminal E is the transcriber's and not the clerk's.

rulings.for_merge: 'PAUL' IS RARE AND THE TOWN HOLDS ONE OF EACH SPELLING. Paul Kingston is corroborated four ways — the Democrat's letter list of 1 April 1834 prints 'Paul Kingston', the ISA land register enters KINGSTON PAUL, and the Andreas and Racine old-settler research passes reach him — while Kingstone, Paul stands on the 1833 tax list alone. A man on the town's tax roll of 1833 who is written to at the post office in 1834 and buys federal ground after is one plausible career.
rulings.against_merge: 'KINGSTONE' OCCURS TWICE IN THE WHOLE CORPUS AND BOTH ARE THE SAME TAX-ROLL LINE. Searched over every deposited text and every extracted claim: the only hits are 'Kingstone, Paul' in voter_lists_1833_1835.txt (line 112) and the genealogytrails transcription of the same roll. The Chicago Democrat prints Kingston five times across 1835 and Kingstone never. The ISA land register — 427 named purchaser spellings, the very corpus T-1001 measured the one-letter fold against — holds KINGSTON PAUL, KINGSTON J T and KINGSTON JOHN T, and no Kingstone at all; and that register holding THREE bearers of the stem is the corpus's own warning that this surname is not unique enough to fold on distance. Moses & Kirkland print Kingston five times and Kingstone never. No title is caught setting both. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.
rulings.note: The land register's refusal of KINGSTON J T against Paul Kingston is already written into the land-sale crosswalk on the forename, and it is the model for this one: the surname reaching is not by itself an identification.

rulings.for_merge: The poll filed 11 August 1834 prints 'Paine, William' (voter_lists_1833_1835.txt line 254) and the Chicago Democrat of 13 August 1834 prints 'Wm. Payne' — one forename, one letter of surname, four days apart, in a town of some hundreds. Neither card carries a trade, an address or a second forename that the other contradicts.
rulings.against_merge: PAINE AND PAYNE ARE BOTH POPULATED SURNAMES IN THIS CORPUS AND THIS TOWN, WHICH IS WHAT THE OTHER NINE PAIRS ARE NOT. The town already holds Seth Paine beside William Paine, and L. W. Payne beside William Payne — two bearers of each spelling, ruled apart by their own forenames. The 1835 poll enters 'Payne, L. W.' (line 343) while the 1834 poll enters 'Paine, William' (line 254), so the town's rolls carry both surnames in their own right. The post office's list of 30 June 1835 prints THREE Paynes in one column — 'Payne Barney', 'Payne Barrey W.', 'Payne Win.' — and no Paine at all. Fergus 1843 prints Paine five times and Payne never; Norris 1844 prints Paine five times. No title reached is caught setting both spellings for one WILLIAM, and where two surnames each have several live bearers a one-letter distance is at its weakest, not its strongest — it is the case T-1001's measurement was about. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.
rulings.note: The only pair of the ten whose two surnames are each independently populated at this town. If any of the six refusals is likely to be right on the merits rather than merely unproven, it is this one.

rulings.for_merge: E. L. Thrall is a documented tradesman of the town — the Democrat of 4 June 1834, column 9, gives him the trade (clothier, tailor) at Charles Taylor's old stand on South Water Street, the business handed to him by its previous owner; Fergus 1843 prints 'Thrall, E. L., clerk, Charles Walker & Co.' and Norris 1844 'Thrall, E. L. clerk, at C. Walker & Co.' The only entry of the stem on any of the town's own rolls is 'Trall, E.L.' on the poll list of 1835 (line 367), and a documented tradesman keeping a South Water Street stand is a man who could be expected on it. The town holds exactly one bearer of each spelling, both 'E. L.'
rulings.against_merge: THE TWO BODIES OF EVIDENCE NEVER TOUCH. Searched over every deposited text and every extracted claim: 'Trall' occurs in exactly two places, the 1835 poll list and genealogytrails' transcription of it — and the Chicago Democrat, Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843, Norris 1844, the Newberry locality cards and Moses & Kirkland set only Thrall, never Trall. The rolls know one spelling, the press and the books know the other, and no publication is caught setting both. That is the Pruyne shape exactly, and it is refused for the same reason. A reader may note the paper's own printing of the trade advertisement reads 'E. L. TRRALL' — a garble that is neither spelling cleanly, and could be read toward either — but a single garbled printing is not a title caught SETTING BOTH, which is what C9 requires, and reading it toward the fold is the reader's willingness, not the printer's inconsistency. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.
rulings.note: The closest of the six to C12's exhaustion: the 1835 poll is a closed roll the document itself bounds, it does not print Thrall, and an independent non-name fact — a documented stand on South Water Street — argues he stood on it. What is missing is the count over the roll's whole T run and the rule that lets C12 reach a surname.

rulings.for_merge: THE STEM IS ALL BUT UNIQUE AND THE TOWN HAS ONE CHARLES OF EACH SPELLING. Charles Wesencraft is documented: the Democrat of 3 December 1833, column 7, prints the marriage of 'Mark Nobles, Esq. of this place, to Miss CHARLOTTE, only daughter of Mr. Charles Wesencraft, late of Buffalo', and his daughter Charlotte stands on her own card; Fergus 1843 prints 'Wesencraft, Charles, carpenter and wagon[maker], cor S. Clinton and W. Monroe' and Norris 1844 repeats the trade. 'Wessencraft, Charles' stands on the 1833 tax list. A carpenter and wagonmaker marrying a daughter into the Noble family in December 1833 is a man the town's tax roll of that year should hold.
rulings.against_merge: NO TITLE SETS BOTH, AND THE DOUBLE-S IS NOT A ONE-OFF SLIP — A SECOND, LATER TITLE SETS IT TOO. Searched over every deposited text: 'Wessencraft' occurs twice in the whole corpus and the two are independent — 'Wessencraft, Charles' on the 1833 tax list (line 159) and 'Wessencraft, Mrs. Jane' on the Second Presbyterian Church roll of 1842-1892 (line 7270). Two documents sixty years apart, neither derived from the other, both doubling the S. Against them the Democrat, Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 set the single S and never the double. The two bodies of evidence do not touch, and a spelling attested by two unrelated sources is exactly the kind a fold should not quietly absorb. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.
rulings.note: Charlotte Wesencraft's card is not touched by this ruling and does not enter it: town_pairs joins only cards whose forename is identical, and the town holds no Charlotte of the double-S spelling.

rulings.for_merge: Alanson Sweet is the only Sweet on a card whose full forename the initial A fits, and he is one of the better-evidenced men in the layer — the 1833 tax roll, the 1834 and 1835 poll lists and the Democrat. On the cards alone this is a one-rival initial, which is the shape T-0839 merges.
rulings.against_merge: The card layer is not the whole corpus. The newspapers also print 'Alon[s]on Sweet', a second full forename the initial A fits just as well, and the identity ladder refuses 'A. Sweet' to BOTH of them under R3 for exactly that reason. Whether Alonson is a second man or a compositor's transposition of Alanson is a reading of the page and not a rule, so the answer decides this cluster and is not in hand. Filed as T-1281.
rulings.note: REACHED BY T-1155, AND IT IS THE REPAIR SHOWING ITS WORK. Before the square-bracket supplies were kept, 'Alon[s]on Sweet' split to the forenames `alon` and `on` and 'A. Sweet' merged onto Alanson unopposed. With the supplied letter back the second printing reads as the full forename Alonson, the ladder sees two rivals, and the Democrat's 'A. Sweet' comes off Alanson's card and stands on its own — refused rather than folded. The card is `undecided` and not merged because the town would otherwise assert a choice between two printings that nobody has made.

rulings.for_merge: One letter inside a five-letter surname with 'Richard' on both, and the two returns are six weeks apart in the scene year itself — the second of them closed on 1 July 1835, the scene date. Neither name is in the corpus under any other forename: 'Allin' is set twice in the whole deposited corpus and both settings are these letter-list impressions.
rulings.against_merge: TWO RETURNS, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. 'Richard B. Allan' stands on the return of 20 May 1835 (chicago_democrat_1835_05_20#c013); 'Allin, Richard' on the return of 1 July 1835 (chicago_democrat_1835_07_01#c004). No return carries both spellings, neither card is an anchor — no trade, no dwelling, no corroborated research on either, both closed no_corroboration by T-0485 and T-0508 — and the middle initial B is printed on one and absent on the other. The office closed two returns six weeks apart and was never asked to set the two spellings together: C9's demonstration is absent and D5's roll is absent with it. D6.

rulings.for_merge: 'John S.' agrees letter for letter including the middle initial, so nothing but the surname's last letters stands between the cards, and both are post-office readings of the same office within ten months.
rulings.against_merge: TWO RETURNS, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. 'John S. Barre' is on the return of 9 July 1834 (chicago_democrat_1834_07_09#c003) and 'John S. Barry' on the return of 20 May 1835 (chicago_democrat_1835_05_20#c013). Neither card is an anchor. BARRY IS A POPULATED SURNAME AT THIS TOWN AND BARRE IS NOT: the town holds barry_j_r, barry_john_s and barry_william, the reading index eight Barry identities, and the deposited corpus sets Barry 59 times against Barre's 14 — of which the Barre hits are the French place name in Moses & Kirkland, not a Chicago family. A surname several men bear is not a slip for one nobody else bears. D6, and the `barry-j` cluster's R3 refusal stands beside it.
rulings.note: This pair and `barry-j`'s R3 answer different questions about the same three cards and neither is disturbed: R3 refuses J. R. against John S. on two printed middle initials, and this refuses John S. Barre against John S. Barry on two returns that never touch.

rulings.for_merge: The initial L agrees with 'Liman', an uncommon forename, and the two returns are six weeks apart — 20 May 1835 and 1 July 1835, the scene date.
rulings.against_merge: TWO RETURNS, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. 'L. G. Curtin' is on the return of 20 May 1835 (#c013), 'Curtis, Liman' on the return of 1 July 1835 (#c004). No return sets both spellings. Neither card is an anchor: T-0483 and T-0510 both closed no_corroboration, and T-0510 recorded that Fergus's death notices carry the surname Curtis with no entry under it bearing these initials. BOTH SPELLINGS ARE POPULATED: the town holds curtin_david beside curtin_l_g and curtis_jacob_s beside curtis_liman, so neither surname is a stem only one man bears. And the fold would have to take the middle initial G on trust, since 'Liman' prints none. D6.

rulings.for_merge: Two five-letter surnames differing in the last letter, both initials beginning W, and both known to the town from one office inside seven weeks. Neither stem is populated: 'Lewie' is set three times in the whole deposited corpus and 'Lewin' twice.
rulings.against_merge: TWO RETURNS, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. 'Lewie, Wm.' is on the return of 1 July 1835 (#c005); 'W. Y. Lewin' on the return of 20 May 1835 (#c013). No return sets both. Neither card is an anchor — T-0482 closed no_corroboration and T-0478 no_corroboration_yet, and neither carries a trade, a street or a household. The forenames agree only at the first letter: 'Wm.' is William written short and 'W. Y.' is an initial with a middle initial the other reading does not have, so the fold is not one letter but a letter and a name. D6.

rulings.for_merge: A terminal l doubled, 'William' and 'Wm.' being the same forename written long and short, and two returns of the same office ten weeks apart. T-0486 found a William Teall of Michigan City arriving in 1834 and licensed to vend merchandise — a real man of the name in the region in the window, which is the strongest external fact either card has.
rulings.against_merge: TWO RETURNS, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. 'William Teal' is on the return of 28 January 1834 (#c001) and 'Wm. Teall' on the return of 1 April 1834 (#c002), the latter read as 'Wm. Teall i 1 Lot Has' — a line the impression damaged. Neither return carries the other spelling; neither card is an anchor; the corpus sets Teal nine times and Teall three, and no setting of either ties to a Chicago household. T-0486's Michigan City man is evidence about a name, not a bridge to this town, and the ticket itself stopped at candidate_identity. D6.

rulings.for_merge: 'F. G.' agrees with 'F. Gantry' initial for initial, the surnames differ by one letter (c against s) in a ten-letter name, and 'Blanshard' is set NOWHERE in the deposited corpus — not once — while Blanchard is set 65 times. A stem with no independent life in the corpus is the shape a mis-set card usually takes.
rulings.against_merge: THE TOWN HOLDS TWO BLANSHARDS, AND NO TITLE SETS BOTH SPELLINGS. Against the corpus silence stands the resident layer: blanshard_f_g and blanshard_g are two cards of that spelling, so within this town the stem is populated in its own right and a fold of one of them says nothing about the other. The readings do not touch: 'Blanchard, F. Gantry' is the poll of 1834 and 'Blanchard, Gantry' the tax list of 1833, with Fergus 1843 ('Francis Gurtrey Blanchard, capitalist, res 45 Wells') and Norris 1844 ('Francis G.') behind them; 'F. G. Blanshard' is the Democrat of 12 November 1834 (#c012) and nothing else. No single printing is caught setting both spellings for one man. D7 — and the `blanchard` cluster's C8 merge of Gantry onto F. Gantry is untouched, because that fold had the directory printing the name whole and this one has nothing of the kind.

rulings.for_merge: A terminal e, 'James' on both, and the two readings are fourteen months apart in one town — the shape a duplicate usually takes, and the spelling of an Irish surname that every clerk of the period set both ways.
rulings.against_merge: BOTH SPELLINGS ARE POPULATED AND THEIR EVIDENCE DOES NOT TOUCH. The reading index holds six Burk identities and five Burke, and the deposited corpus sets Burk 18 times and Burke 65 — two live surnames, which is the case a one-letter distance is at its weakest in (T-1001). 'James Burk' is the post-office return of 28 January 1834 (#c001) and nothing else; 'Burke, James' is the 1833 tax list of the Town of Chicago and, later, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 — a letter list against a tax roll, D7's own example of two instruments that never touch. No printing sets both spellings for one man. D7.

rulings.for_merge: C against R at the head of a surname is a one-letter distance the exact test cannot see, and the initial J agrees with John.
rulings.against_merge: THE COLLINS CARD IS A NAMED MAN WITH A TRADE AND THE ROLLINS CARD IS A DIFFERENT ENTRY IN THE SAME PAPER. J. H. Collins is James H. Collins, attorney: Fergus 1843 gives 'Collins, James H., attorney (Butterfield & C), res 15 Lake', Norris 1844 the same man at Lake near Wabash, the Democrat prints him from 28 January 1834 to 5 August 1835, and T-0509 corroborated the identity through the Papers of Abraham Lincoln. 'Rollins, John, Jr.' is the Democrat of 17 September 1834 (#c002) — a different issue, a junior, and no trade. The town holds rollins_charles beside rollins_john, so Rollins is a populated surname here; Collins is set 204 times in the corpus and Rollins five. Nothing folds a documented attorney onto another man's son on one letter. D7.

rulings.for_merge: The initial L agrees with Liman and both cards are Chicago readings of the summer of 1835.
rulings.against_merge: ONE ISSUE SETS BOTH SPELLINGS IN TWO DIFFERENT COLUMNS, WHICH IS EVIDENCE AGAINST AND NOT FOR. The Democrat of 1 July 1835 prints 'Curtis, Liman' in the post-office return at column 4 and 'L. Curtiss' at column 13 of the same issue. A compositor who set Curtis in one column and Curtiss in another that day was distinguishing two names, not wavering over one; C9 asks for a printing caught setting both spellings FOR ONE MAN and this is a printing caught keeping them apart. L. G. Curtiss is besides set 'L. G. Curtiss' on 22 July and 'Curtiss, L. G.' on 5 August 1835, three settings that never drop the second s, and the town holds curtiss_j beside him. The middle initial G is printed on the Curtiss side and absent on Liman's. D7.

rulings.for_merge: A terminal e and an initial that agrees with John, and the Greene card is the best anchored card the pool touches: Major John Greene, in command at Fort Dearborn on the scene date, with quarters and a post in the record.
rulings.against_merge: THE ANCHOR IS ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE FOLD, AND THAT IS X2's POINT. 'J. Green' is the 1835 poll list and the American of 13 June 1835 (#c013); Major John Greene is Andreas and the fort literature, with no letter-list or poll reading at all. The initial J attaches to 'John' only because the candidate test folded the surname first, so the forename inference is a fact about the rest of the town and not evidence about the reading — the direction T-0697 refused. GREEN IS POPULATED AND GREENE IS NOT: the town holds green_damel_m, green_j and green_mary, the reading index thirteen Green identities against one Greene, and no Green of the town is a John. No printing is caught setting both spellings for one man, and the fold would put a serving army major onto a town poll roll on the strength of one letter. D7.

rulings.for_merge: H and V are one letter apart to a distance and one glyph apart to a worn impression, 'John' is identical, and both readings are the Democrat inside sixteen months.
rulings.against_merge: THREE DIFFERENT ISSUES, AND NEITHER SPELLING EVER SHARES ONE. 'John Hale' is the Democrat of 16 April 1834 (#c005) and 'Hale, John' the return of 1 July 1835 (#c005); 'Vale, John' is the Democrat of 5 August 1835 (#c006). No issue sets both. Both stems are alive in the corpus — Hale 83 settings, Vale 33 — and neither card is an anchor: no trade, no street, no household on either. H against V is not the substitution a period compositor's case makes, and the reading index holds three Hale identities to Vale's one. D7.

rulings.for_merge: Hoit and Hoyt are one surname's two current spellings in 1830s America, 'Thomas' is identical, and the Democrat carries both cards.
rulings.against_merge: EACH SPELLING HAS A SECOND BEARER AT THIS TOWN. The resident layer holds hoit_sarah beside hoit_thomas and hoyt_l_g beside hoyt_thomas: two families, not one, which is precisely the Paine/Payne case D7 was extended over. The printings do not touch — 'Hoit, Thomas' is the Democrat of 24 September 1834 (#c002); 'Thomas Hoyt' the Democrat of 17 December 1833 (#c008) and the 1835 poll list — and no issue or roll sets both spellings. T-0510 stopped this pair at candidate_identity and recorded that Fergus's death notices carry the surname Hoit with no entry under it bearing the initial. D7.

rulings.for_merge: THIS IS THE STRONGEST MERGE ARGUMENT IN THE FORTY-THREE AND IT IS RECORDED IN FULL. Two consecutive directories print the same man's trade, firm and street under the two spellings: Fergus 1843 has 'Loyd, Alexander, carpenter and builder, (L., Blakesley & Co.), res 52 Wells [4th mayor…]' and Norris 1844 has 'Lloyd, Alexander, builder, of L. Blakesly & Co. res Wells b Lake and Randolph sts'. Same given name, same trade, same firm, same street. Moses & Kirkland's History sets both spellings inside one work and for one man — v1 indexes 'Loyd, Alexander, 102' and prints 'Alexander Lloyd' at four places, v2 prints 'Alexander Loyd, Mayor of the city' and 'with Alexander Lloyd for the building of…' — and the Democrat prints 'A. Lloyd' on 29 October 1834 and 'A. Loyd' on 19 November 1834, three weeks apart. The firm and the address are NON-NAME discriminators and they agree; the town is carrying its own fourth mayor as two residents.
rulings.against_merge: AND IT IS STILL REFUSED HERE, BECAUSE NO LANDED RULE REACHES IT AND THIS PASS MAY NOT WRITE ONE. C9 wants one publication caught setting both spellings for one man INSIDE THE WINDOW: the Democrat's two settings are two different issues, and Moses & Kirkland is an 1895 history describing 1840, so the catch is outside the window and its v2 index besides carries a 'Lloyd, Alexander C., 384' whose middle initial neither card has. C11 is the rule this evidence actually fits — two spellings discharging one documented office, tied by a non-name discriminator — but C11 as drafted requires THE SURNAME TO AGREE LETTER FOR LETTER and varies the forename, and it is the surname that varies here. That asymmetry is the same one C14 was written to fix for C12, and fixing it for C11 is a new MERGE rule. T-1027 is explicit that the one-letter pool may not be closed by widening the join, and a merge is a card DELETION that moves the town's count; drawing a rule to make one is the owner's call and not this pass's. So the argument is kept verbatim, as D7 requires, and the cards stay two.
rulings.note: WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT, stated so the next pass does not re-derive this: either one in-window printing — an issue of the Democrat or the American setting Lloyd and Loyd for the builder — or C11 drawn onto the surname as C14 was drawn onto C12's, on the firm 'L. Blakesley & Co.' and the Wells Street address that Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 already agree on. This is the one pair in the pool where the second is worth asking for.

rulings.for_merge: A terminal y lost, 'John' identical, and 'Ludb' is set NOWHERE in the deposited corpus while Ludby is set three times — the profile of a truncated reading rather than a family. John Ludby is a documented man: Fergus 1843 has 'Ludby, John, soap and candle maker, South Branch, 3 miles south [died January 24, 1872, aged 78.]', and the Democrat prints him on 19 November 1834.
rulings.against_merge: THE TWO INSTRUMENTS NEVER TOUCH. 'John Ludb' is the post-office return of 2 July 1834 (#c029) and nothing else; John Ludby is the Democrat of 19 November 1834 (#c006) and Fergus 1843 — a letter list against a newspaper and a directory, D7's own example. No issue and no return is caught setting both spellings, and the letter-list card is not an anchor: T-0482 closed it no_corroboration. The fold is admissible in shape and has no demonstration behind it, which is exactly what D7 is for. `for_merge` is kept because a later reading of the 2 July 1834 return's image could show the terminal y in the impression and close this.

rulings.for_merge: 'Niles' is an uncommon forename and it is identical on both, and the surnames differ in one letter that a worn impression confuses.
rulings.against_merge: TWO ISSUES OF ONE PAPER, NEITHER SETTING BOTH, AND ROSE IS POPULATED HERE. 'Niles Rose' is the post-office return of 2 July 1834 (#c031); 'Niles Ross' the Democrat of 16 April 1834 (#c012) — two and a half months and two instruments apart, and no printing carries both spellings. The town holds rose_ruel beside rose_niles; the reading index holds seven Rose identities and five Ross, and the corpus sets Rose 151 times and Ross 50. Neither card is an anchor and T-0484 closed the letter-list side no_corroboration with 'no discriminator' written against it. D7.

rulings.for_merge: A stray terminal s, and the anchor side is one of the best-documented men in the layer: Giles Spring, attorney of S. & Goodrich, res 62 Adams, on the 1834 poll, the 1835 poll as 'Spring, G.', and in the Democrat as 'G. Spring' and 'Spring, G.'. The initial G agrees, the town holds exactly one Spring and one Springs, and a man the paper already prints under a bare G is the obvious referent for 'G. Springs'.
rulings.against_merge: NO ISSUE SETS BOTH SPELLINGS, AND THE SPRINGS STEM IS NOT EMPTY. 'G. Springs' is the Democrat of 29 October 1834 (#c008); Giles Spring's own Democrat settings are 28 January 1834 (#c006), 3 September 1834 (#c005) and 12 November 1834 (#c008) — four different issues of one paper and not one of them sets Spring and Springs together. The corpus sets Springs 53 times in its own right. C9's demonstration is what is missing and nothing else, which is D7 exactly; the anchor makes the fold attractive and D7 is the rule that says an attractive fold with no page is still a refusal.

rulings.for_merge: One letter in the stem of a twelve-letter Dutch surname, 'Henry' identical, and the Vanderbogart card is documented as a man: Fergus's old-settler notices print 'Bogart, Dr. Henry Van der' and 'Van der Bogart, Dr. Henry' with a death of 8 April 1835, and the Democrat sets 'H. Van Den Bogart' on 4 February 1834 and 'H. Vanderbogart' on 20 May 1835. 'Vanderbogert' is set four times in the corpus and nowhere outside this town's own records. The town holds exactly one of each.
rulings.against_merge: THE PARTICLE IS ALREADY RULED AND THE STEM IS NOT. T-0842's C7 merge in the `vanderbogart` cluster folded Van Den against Van der on the printer's own practice, read at the Democrat of 4 February 1834 — that is the PARTICLE. What separates these two cards is a vowel inside the stem, a against e, and no printing reached is caught setting both: 'Vanderbogert, Henry' is the 1833 tax list and nothing else, and no issue, roll or notice carries the two spellings together. C7's demonstration does not transfer from the particle to the stem — that is C9's question and C9's page is missing. D7.

rulings.for_merge: S against T is one letter, 'John' is identical, and the middle initial L is printed on one card and absent on the other, which is M3's shape and not a contradiction.
rulings.against_merge: WILSON IS ONE OF THE MOST POPULATED SURNAMES IN THE CORPUS AND THE TWO BODIES OF EVIDENCE NEVER MEET. 'John Wilson' is the post-office return of 28 January 1834 (#c001) and two separate 1840 census households (229:2 and 239:4) — the census itself holding two John Wilsons, which is the town telling us the name is not unique; 'Wilton, John L.' is the 1835 poll list alone. Wilson is set 314 times in the deposited corpus against Wilton's eight, and the reading index holds 24 Wilson identities. A letter list and a census against a poll roll is D7's 'two instruments that never touch', and no printing sets both spellings. D7.

rulings.for_merge: One letter at the head of a forename on a surname that agrees letter for letter, and the Byram card is documented: Byram King, hardware merchant, in the Democrat of 9 July 1834 (#c020), 23 July 1834 as 'Byra[m]' and 3 September 1834 (#c022), in the 1840 census at 207:4 and in Fergus's old-settler notices. The paper is demonstrably unsteady about this very forename — T-1027's own table records the printings BYRA, BYRAM, BYRKAM and BYWAM.
rulings.against_merge: BYRAM AND HYRAM ARE TWO GIVEN NAMES, NOT TWO SPELLINGS OF ONE. Hyram is Hiram, among the commonest forenames in the corpus; Byram is rare. The paper's instability about Byram runs to its last letters — BYRA, BYRKAM, BYWAM — and never to its first, which is the letter that would have to move. The printings do not touch: every Byram reading is the Democrat of 1834 or later records, and 'Hyram King' is a single reading in the American of 20 June 1835 (#c016). KING IS THE MOST POPULATED SURNAME IN THIS POOL — the town holds seven King cards, including a king_byron whose forename is a third variant nobody proposes folding — and no printing sets Byram and Hyram for one man. D8.

rulings.for_merge: The surname agrees letter for letter and the forenames differ in one letter, which is all the one-letter test looks at.
rulings.against_merge: ONE IS A MAN AND THE OTHER IS A WOMAN, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE ANSWER. Mark Noble, Esq. is the 1833 tax list and two of Fergus's old-settler death notices; 'Mary Noble' is the Democrat of 3 December 1833 (#c007). Mark and Mary are two given names of different sex, not two spellings of one name, so C10's first condition — that nothing but the SPELLING of the forename stands between the cards — is not merely undemonstrated but false. The town holds four Nobles (noble_john, noble_mark, noble_mary, noble_william_b) and the surname is set 161 times in the corpus. No printing sets both, and none could: a fold here would put a woman's reading on a man's card. This is the clearest refusal in the forty-three and it is recorded so the distance is never trusted again on a forename.
rulings.note: It is the pair that most cheaply demonstrates why the one-letter pool is not a worklist. Mark/Mary and Foot/Foote are the same distance.

rulings.for_merge: Jeddiah and Jedidiah are one biblical forename written short and long, the surname agrees letter for letter, the town holds only these two Wooleys, and T-0481 found the La Salle land-sale records listing a Jeddiah Wooley repeatedly on 16-17 June 1835 — a fortnight before the scene date.
rulings.against_merge: THE TAX ENTRY IS A JUNIOR, SO THE TOWN HELD TWO MEN OF THE LONGER NAME. The 1833 tax list reads 'Wooley, Jedidiah Jr.', and a roll that troubles to write Jr. is a roll telling us a senior of the same name existed; the letter-list 'Jeddiah Wooley' of 2 July 1834 (#c034) could be either of them, and a fold would have to choose. No printing sets both spellings: a tax roll against a post-office return, which never touch. Neither card is an anchor — no trade, no street, no household on either. D8, and the Jr. is the fact that keeps it there.

rulings.for_merge: One interior vowel in a four-letter surname with 'Frank' identical, both readings from the town's own voter lists a year apart, and neither stem otherwise populated at this town: one Dell card and one Dill card, nothing else.
rulings.against_merge: TWO DIFFERENT ROLLS OF ONE TRANSCRIPTION, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. Both cards cite `chicago_voter_lists_1833_1835_irad`, so a grep finds both spellings in one file — but the file bundles four separate closed rolls and the two readings are on two of them: 'Dell, Frank' is the poll filed 11 August 1834 (voter_lists_1833_1835.txt line 202) and 'Dill, Frank' the 1835 poll list (line 305). No roll enters both spellings, so C9's demonstration is absent; no roll enters both as separate entries either, so D5's refusal is unavailable. Neither card is an anchor. D9.

rulings.for_merge: THE SPELLING MOVES AND THE TOWN MOVES WITH IT. The 1833 tax list enters 'Foot, John' at line 82 and 'Foot, Starr' at line 83; the poll filed 11 August 1834 enters 'Foote, John' at line 208 and 'Foote, Star' at line 209; the 1835 poll enters 'Foot, John' again at line 309. Two men, adjacent on three successive rolls, changing spelling together and back again — which is a clerk's hand varying, not four households appearing and disappearing in pairs. On resemblance plus pattern this is the most merge-like pair in the forty-three after Lloyd/Loyd.
rulings.against_merge: AND NO ONE ROLL SETS BOTH, WHICH IS WHAT C9 ASKS FOR. The three rolls are internally consistent: tax 1833 sets FOOT twice, poll 1834 sets FOOTE twice, poll 1835 sets FOOT. The variation is between rolls and never inside one, so the printer is never caught — and a shared source id is not a shared printing. No roll enters both spellings as separate entries either, so D5 does not refuse harder and does not acquit. Neither card is an anchor: foot_john is the 1835 poll and the 1833 tax list with no trade, foote_john the 1834 poll alone. D9, and the pattern is kept verbatim because it is the argument a later page would only have to confirm.
rulings.note: The pair `foot-foote-starr` below is the same three rolls read at the adjacent line, and the two rulings stand or fall together. If either is ever folded, both must be.

rulings.for_merge: The second half of the pattern above, and this side carries the documented man: 'Foot, Starr' is the 1833 tax list, the Democrat of 3 September 1834 (#c007), Fergus 1843 ('Foot, Starr, teamster, 180 Clark, cor Monroe [died June, 1862. a 62.]') and Norris 1844 ('Foot, S. teamster, corner of Clark and Monroe sts'), while 'Foote, Star' is the poll of 1834 alone — the same roll that set his neighbour John as Foote.
rulings.against_merge: AND THE SAME ANSWER FOR THE SAME REASON. rulings.for_merge: THE TWO SURNAMES ARE ONE WORD. The Democrat of 2 July 1834 (#c009) sets "A. M'Gregor" — with the Scots apostrophe — and this project's own normaliser rendered it `mgregor`, which is why a one-letter test sees a difference at all. M'Gregor and McGregor are the same surname, so what actually stands between the cards is the initial A against the forename 'Ashor' of 'McGregor, Ashor' on the poll filed 11 August 1834. The town holds no other McGregor of any spelling, so the initial has exactly one candidate — which is C2's shape, an initial onto its one full forename, and C2 is a MERGE rule.
rulings.against_merge: AND THE QUESTION IS NOT THIS PAIR'S. The obstacle is a normalisation: the two card ids differ because `M'Gregor` was folded to `mgregor` rather than to `mcgregor`, and deciding that is a change to how the project renders Scots and Irish particles across the whole layer — the same class of decision C7 settled for Dutch and French particles, and not one to settle from inside one pair of cards. Ruling MERGE here would land a fold whose real warrant is a rule nobody has written; ruling DISTINCT would assert two McGregors the corpus does not show. So both readings are kept and the pair is recorded AMBIGUOUS under U2 — the finished answer T-1291's owner asked for, not a deferral. NO TICKET IS FILED, by that ticket's fourth acceptance clause.
rulings.note: The apostrophe class is worth one rule someday and it is worth naming here so the next pass does not re-derive it: M', Mc and Mac in one surname, the way Van Den and Van der were. That is an observation, not a ticket.
